topic: Computational Modeling of Electronic Energy Transfer Between Silicon Quantum Dots Using Foerster Theory
title: Computational Modeling of Electronic Energy Transfer Between Silicon Quantum Dots Using Foerster Theory
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Nicolas Vinson, Harvy Freitag and David A. Micha
abstract: The efficiency of photovoltaic devices is limited by material constraints. A thorough investigation of the nanostructure, composition, and behavior of such devices is essential to the advanced development of solar energy-conversion materials for practical use. Herein lies the motivation to characterize the nanostructures of silicon quantum dots, which hold the potential to greatly improve the theoretical efficiency of current photovoltaic devices. In this study, the photodynamic properties of crystalline and amorphous silicon quantum dot systems doped with a phosphorous or aluminum atom, or with an adsorbed silver atom, and a combination thereof were characterized using the computational method of time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT). The systems of interest were saturated Si 29 and Si 3 5 structures. The approximations of the model for calculating system property trends have yielded consistent results with empirical studies of solid-state electronic structures. Our model allows calculation of the rate of photon energy transfer between two structurally identical doped silicon quantum dots. Using the Foerster theory of electronic energy transfer, the photoexcitation energy transfer rates were computed by introducing the electric dipole-dipole interaction. The strength of the dipole interaction is associated with the transition probability of states, and is characterized by the oscillator strengths for such spectral transitions. Spatial orientation of the electric dipole moments was chosen to relate energy transfer rates to the geometric configuration of the coupled systems. Our results show that it is possible to configure the structure and relative orientation of quantum dots to obtain desired rates of electronic energy transfer. topic: Controlling Photo-Stimulated Biological Proton Pumping with an Electrochromic Window
title: Controlling Photo-Stimulated Biological Proton Pumping with an Electrochromic Window
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Steven Wolf, Leo Small, Virginia Vandelinder, George Bachand and Erik Spoerke
abstract: Electrochromic materials, such as tungsten oxide (WO 3 ), can undergo voltage-triggered changes in color and optical density, potentially valuable characteristics for applications such as energy control for buildings or window tint for privacy. Using external voltage to control the oxidation state of tungsten in WO 3 , the optical absorbance of this material can be reversibly tuned, evidenced by a visible transformation from yellow to blue. This change in absorbance overlaps with the absorbance of the light-activated biological proton pump, bacteriorhodopsin (BR). BR absorbs light at 568 nm and, in turn, pumps protons across a lipid membrane. Here we explore the use of electrochromic WO 3 thin film windows to control the activity of BR proteins incorporated into lipid vesicles. Specifically, we utilize solution-phase chemistry to create WO 3 thin films on transparent conductive substrates. Electrochemical windows were created from these thin film substrates, and using cyclic voltammetry in a range of positive 1 V and -3 V with respect to an Ag/AgCl electrode, the absorbance of the WO 3 windows was varied. These windows were then used to regulate light delivery to BR-containing vesicles in aqueous solution. BR activity, as a function of tunable WO 3 absorbance was determined by monitoring changes in solution pH induced by proton pumping of the BR proteins. This approach represents a creative integration of electrochromic materials with photo-activated proteins to create a programmable biological response. Continued research in this area may lead to the development of new, innovative material hybrids for emerging technologies.

topic: Using Amphiphilic Alpha-Helical Peptides to Stabilize Microbubbles
title: Using Amphiphilic Alpha-Helical Peptides to Stabilize Microbubbles
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Pierre Desir
abstract: Using amphiphilic alpha-helical peptides to stabilize microbubbles Pierre Desir 1,* , Joseph Badami, and Raymond Tu Department of Chemical Engineering, The City College of New York, New York, NY 10031 Abstract Microbubbles are gaseous particles usually encapsulated by a lipid monolayer and dispersed in an aqueous solution. These particles have been engineered to implement various types of targeting molecules onto their surface for drug delivery. We investigated how the partitioning of alpha-helical peptides onto the bubble interface influenced the overall structure of the system in terms of stability and size of the microbubbles. It follows that implementing such molecules on the microbubble encapsulation creates an anchor on the lipid monolayer, which can prevent its collapse and the rapid disintegration of the bubble structure. Two fluorescent peptides, Peptide 2.5 and Peptide 6.0, were synthesized to have the same amino acid composition and three positive charge residues with different charge separations. The encapsulation of the microbubbles was made of two lipids, DPPC and DPPA, in the respective mass ratios of 5:1 and 5:2 for the two samples prepared. The relative amount of peptide bound to the bubble interface was determined by spectroscopic measurements of its molecular constituents using a spectrophotometer. For the two compositions of the bubble encapsulation used, the relative amount of Peptide 2.5 partitioned changed from 16.42% to 16.24% and that of Peptide 6.0 from 22.27% to 28.89% as the concentration of DPPA increased. Moreover, Circular Dichroism was used to analyze the secondary structure of the peptides once integrated on the liposome surface. Thereon, the secondary structure of Peptide 2.5 changed from an alpha-helical to a beta sheet configuration while Peptide 6.0 conserved its alpha-helical structure after binding. It followed that the charge separation on the peptides influenced their relative partitioning to the bubble interface and their configuration once partitioned. Furthermore, the influence of peptide partitioning on microbubble size was assessed by measuring the mean diameter of these structures under laser scattering for a period of 20 minutes. The control bubbles had an average size of 579 nm. Peptide 2.5 partitioned onto microbubbles with an average size of 492 nm while Peptide 6.0 produced microbubbles of 545 nm in size. Overall, the microbubbles displayed a relatively constant size with the peptides partitioned onto the interface, which denoted that the peptides stabilized these structures.

topic: The Effects of Calcium on the Structure of Zwitterionic Lipid Bilayers
title: The Effects of Calcium on the Structure of Zwitterionic Lipid Bilayers
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: William Zygmunt and Jeffrey J. Potoff
abstract: Calcium is one of many different ions found in the extracellular fluid and in the cytosol of the cells of the body. Calcium has a major effect on the cellular environment and especially the lipid bilayer that encases it. Calcium also has major implications when discussing the structure of the bilayer and the fusion of cells to various other vesicles. Molecular simulation using the CHARMM (ver. 36) force field parameters and the molecular dynamics simulation engine NAMD (ver. 2.9) were performed on lipid bilayers composed of the zwitterionic lipid 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC) in the presence of various ions to demonstrate what effects these ions have on bilayer structure. Systems of sodium ions, calcium ions, and systems without ions were simulated under isobaric and isothermal conditions. Results show that both ions decrease the area per lipid and increase the order parameter of the lipid tails. This data directly shows the effects of calcium on the lipid bilayer structure and its implications for the cell as a whole.

topic: Thermal Release Tape Method for Transfer and Characterization of Hexagonal Boron Nitride Grown By Metal Precipitation
title: Thermal Release Tape Method for Transfer and Characterization of Hexagonal Boron Nitride Grown By Metal Precipitation
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Yichao Zhang, Timothy Hoffman and James H Edgar
abstract: Thermal Release Tape Method for Transfer and Characterization of Hexagonal Boron Nitride Grown by Metal Precipitation Yichao Zhang, Timothy B. Hoffman, James H. Edgar Kansas State University, Department of Chemical Engineering, Durland Hall, Manhattan, KS 66506 Abstract Neutron detectors have shown an increasing importance in homeland security and nuclear non-proliferation, as they are capable of detecting nuclear weapons material. [1]. He-3 is currently the most widely used neutron detector material, however, due to the shortage of He-3 gas, as well as difficulty in inconvenience of transporting the device and high voltage operation requirement, there is a need for better alternatives [2]. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a compound semiconductor material that has shown potential in several applications, including use as a neutron detector, as. B-10, an isotope of boron, reacts strongly with thermal neutrons, making it a possible choice for solid state neutron detector material [3]. Several methods have been developed to produce hBN single crystal for neutron detector devices, including both CVD and bulk growth techniques. The goal of this research is to develop a method to transfer hBN produced from metal flux growth using a Ni-Cr solvent, thus allowing for material characterization free of the metal substrate. This research has implemented two ways of transferring hBN crystal, one of which is using thermal release tape to transfer thick layers of hBN crystal for fabrication of hBN detector devices. The other method is mechanical exfoliation via scotch tape, which yields much thinner layers of hBN crystal. Microscopy techniques, such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM) and optical microscopy are used in characterizing these crystals. Thermal release tape has the unique property that it has adhesion that can be deactivated through the application of heat. The tape used in this research has a release temperature of 150 ° C. The transfer process was as follows. First, the tape was cut into 1 cm by 1cm pieces for use. The handle substrate for the crystal (glass or sapphire) was cleaned by three successive five-minute cycles of sonication using with trichloroethylene (TCE) followed by acetone and then methanol, followed by drying in air. The thermal release tape piece was pressed onto the hBN crystal for ten seconds then carefully removed, extracting the crystal from the metal substrate onto the tape. Then the tape was manually pressed onto the clean handle substrate, contacting the hBN with the handle substrate. The substrate-tape complex was then soaked in acetone for five seconds, and placed tape-side up onto a hot plate heated to the tape release temperature (150 °C) After a few minutes, the tape began to release and peel back from the substrate, as can be seen in Figure 1. At this time, the tape could then be carefully removed, leaving the hBN crystals on the handle substrate, completing the transfer process. Second transfer method, mechanical exfoliation, was first developed for the production of graphene, but can be applied to hBN due to their structural similarities. The mechanical exfoliation in graphene breaks the weak interlayer Van der Waals forces that hold the stacked layers of graphite together, causing the formation of monolayer graphene with each successive step of exfoliation [4]. This research has adopted the same method, but applied it to produce thin-layer hBN , not monolayer, for the measurement of crystal properties. The crystal flakes which fail to transfer during the thermal release tape method are recollected used in the mechanical exfoliation process. An adequate amount (4 mm 2 ) of crystal is off-centered on a length of 10 cm long strip of scotch tape, with. The tape is then folded in half and pulled apart 5 times, causing the crystal to be exfoliated and spread on the tape. After the exfoliating is completed, tape is pressed onto a handle substrate cleaned by the same method as described in the thermal release tape transferring method. The substrate is left in contact overnight with the scotch tape to allow for crystal release. After 24 hours, the tape is removed from the substrate and soaked in acetone for two hours to remove the tape residue. The key of this process is the selection of handle substrate and removal of the tape residue. hBN has been transferred onto several handle substrates for optical characterization and electrical characterization. Exfoliated hBN has very low optical contrast, making it difficult to observe under an optical microscope when on a transparent substrate [5]. Experiments have been performed on glass, quartz, SiO 2 thermal oxide on Si, silicon carbide, and sapphire substrates to determine the substrate with high contrast and rate of transfer. Exfoliation was also performed on an aluminum substrate for measurement of electrical properties. Residual tape residue is a problem for characterization because it worsens surface roughness, affecting AFM measurement. Several methods have been explored to remove this residue, including soaking in TCE for 24 hours and thermal degradation of the residue under H 2 / Ar gas at 500 °C [6].Of these methods, thermal treatment of samples under H 2 / Ar gas at 500 °C has shown to be most successful in removing remaining tape residue. topic: Oxygen Carrier Development for Carbon Dioxide Capture from Fossil Fuels
title: Oxygen Carrier Development for Carbon Dioxide Capture from Fossil Fuels
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Ziren Wang
abstract: The release of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) from burning of fossil fuel has caused significant energy and environmental concerns. Carbon capture is a process to prevent the emissions of CO 2 , a major source of greenhouse gases. Among the various carbon capture techniques, chemical looping combustion (CLC) has shown promise to be an efficient and effective method for CO 2 capture. The CLC process includes one reduction and one oxidation steps. In the reduction step, oxygen carrier reacts with fuel such as methane in the fuel reactor to reduce oxygen carrier, and produce a gaseous mixture of concentrated CO 2 and water vapor. The oxidation step occurs in a separate air reactor where the reduced oxygen carrier and air react, regenerating oxygen carrier and producing heat. To achieve a high performance of CLC process, the selection of appropriate oxygen carriers is crucial. An oxygen carrier is usually composed of two parts: a metal oxide and a support. The metal oxide participates directly in CLC process, and the support can enhance the reduction-oxidation (redox) reactivity of the oxygen carrier by reducing the energy barrier for oxygen anion and electron conductions. It has been suggested from the literature that barium cerium ferrite (BCF), calcium titanium ferrite (CTF) and lanthanum strontium ferrite (LSF) have good conductivities of oxygen anions and electrons. When they are used as the support part, we found that the redox activities of the ferrite base oxygen carriers are enhanced. The prepared catalyst samples are analyzed and observed by X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) and Scanning electron microscopy (SEM). From the obtained experimental data, CTF exhibited satisfactory stability, low cost, and good reactivity. Therefore, CTF can be used as a suitable oxygen carrier support in CLC process for CO 2 capture and benefit environmental sustainability. In this poster, I will present XRD patterns and SEM images of experimental samples to further illustrate the results. topic: Plasmon Resonances in Bimetallic Nanostructures: The Role of Temperature and Core/Shell Architecture
title: Plasmon Resonances in Bimetallic Nanostructures: The Role of Temperature and Core/Shell Architecture
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Jayde Aufrecht, Holly Zarick, William Erwin, Chanse Hungerford, Andrew Coppola, Philippe Fauchet, Cary Pint and Rizia Bardhan
abstract: Bimetallic nanostructures are of significant technological interest due to their ability to synergistically combine properties of two distinct metals giving rise to multimodal characteristics. In this work, we have synthesized Au@Ag bimetallic nanostructures of three different geometries (nanocubes, nanopyramids, and nanorods) and investigated the role of thermal induction in controlling the nanostructure morphological evolution and the corresponding impact on the optical resonances. By increasing the reaction temperature from 28 °C to 150 °C we observe a red-shift in the plasmon resonance of the nanopyramids followed by a blue-shift at temperatures above boiling point of water; however, no appreciable shift was observed in the optical resonance of the nanocubes. The observed behavior was attributed to a combination of phase retardation effects, stability and critical micelle concentration of ligands, and energetics of the different crystal planes. We also investigated the formation dynamics and observed a sigmoidal growth at lower temperatures relative to an exponential growth at higher temperatures. The activation energy was calculated from the growth dynamics and the rate of nucleation was correlated to the reductive ability of ascorbic acid. Finally we also investigated the effect of core to shell ratio in determining the morphological evolution of bimetallic nanostructures.

topic: Self-Folding of Pre-Strained Polymer Sheets Via Light
title: Self-Folding of Pre-Strained Polymer Sheets Via Light
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Brandi Shaw, Ying Liu, Jan Genzer and Michael D. Dickey
abstract: Self-folding is a self-assembly process that causes a predefined 2D template to fold into a desired 3D structure with high fidelity.1 Self-folding can be applied in the fields of actuation, sensors, and packaging. We have developed a simple method of self-folding that uses pre-defined ink “hinges” printed onto pre-stressed polymer sheets via a desk top printer. The ink absorbs external light, causing the area underneath the hinge to heat up and relax the strain in the hinge regions gradually across the sheet thickness. This process results in folding the sheet at the hinge region. We will demonstrate that sequential folding of multiple hinges on the same sample can be programmed by changing the light source and ink color of the hinge. We have successfully employed this strategy to produce complex origami shapes. References 1. T.G. Leong, A.M. Zarafshar, D.H. Gracias, Small, 2010, 6, 792.

abstract: Impressive Swelling Abilities of Polymerized Imidazolium-based Ionic Liquid in Polar Organic Solvents Mary Allison Andrews, W. Jeffrey Horne, Jason E. Bara Department of Chemical Engineering, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, 35487 Advisor: E. Jason Bara Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL, 35487 Abstract Solvent absorption tests were done with polymers made with the C1 monomer (methylimidazolium monomer with a bis((trifluoromethyl)sulfonyl)amide anion), which is a room temperature ionic liquid (RTIL). We varied the amount of initiator added to the monomer before polymerization, in order to determine the effects, specifically in cross-linking. This imidazolium-based ionic liquid, once polymerized, absorbs certain organic solvents. As the weight percent initiator that was added to the monomer increased, the amount of organic solvent absorbed by the resulting polymer also increased. Under certain conditions, Dimethyl Sulfoxide swelled the polymers over 200 times their original size. This incredible behavior is believed to be due to a decrease in cross-linking occurring with the added initiator, as well as longer polymer chains being formed. Allowing for more space in-between polymer chains that solvent can be absorbed into.

title: Self-Assembled Nanoparticle Anti-Glare Coatings for Glass Substrates

abstract: Self-Assembled Nanoparticle Anti-glare Coatings for Glass Substrates Anti-reflection coatings (ARC's) are widely used in photovoltaic and many other optoelectronic applications. A large variety of techniques currently exist in fabricating ARC's, but unfortunately many of them suffer from being very expensive or time consuming. Here we introduce a novel self-assembled method to fabricate ARC's on glass substrates. Both sides of the substrates are easily coated with a closely packed monolayer of silica nanoparticles using electrostatic forces. The coatings produced were extremely uniform and had a minimum reflection less than 1% for a broad range of visible and near-infrared wavelengths. This method is simple and scalable that lowers reflection less than 1% which is highly promising for applications ranging from highly efficient solar cells and photo detectors to flat panel displays.

topic: Modeling Three Phase Boundary Density of Infiltrated Solid Oxide Fuel Cell Electrodes
title: Modeling Three Phase Boundary Density of Infiltrated Solid Oxide Fuel Cell Electrodes
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Andrew J. L. Reszka, Ryan C. Snyder and Michael D Gross
abstract: Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (SOFCs) are electrochemical devices, characterized by their solid, ceramic electrolytes that directly oxidize a fuel to produce electricity with low emissions and high efficiency. For the fuel cell to be functional the electrodes must have porosity for fuel transport through the cell, oxygen ion conductivity to transport the oxidizing agent to the fuel, electrical conductivity to transport electrons from the reaction, and three phase boundary (TPB) sites to enable chemical reaction. TPB sites occur at the intersections of electrical conductor particles, ceramic particles and empty space so that the oxidation reaction may occur at a site with the electrons, oxidizing agent and fuel all present. Recent work has shown that electrode fabrication by infiltration of electronic conductor/oxidation catalyst particles into an oxygen ion rich porous backbone provides excellent performance while decreasing the amount of conductor material necessary as compared with other fabrication methods. Infiltrated electrodes also allow for flexibility in composition and structure of the electrodes. This fabrication method, however, has many design parameters whose impact on the resulting cell’s performance is not fully understood. Experimentally exploring these parameters is very time consuming, thus a modeling effort can help to guide the desired experiments. In this work, we show a model for the design process of a SOFC and the corresponding determination of both electrical conductivity and TPB density for the formulated electrodes. The model is based on the underlying physics of the electrode fabrication process. The fabrication process begins with the slurry formation and film creation, followed by pore former combustion, ceramic particle sintering and conducting particle infiltration. After formulation, results can be determined from cells with appropriate size to mimic an infinitely sized cell to get consistent data. Some highlighted results include a TPB density decrease with increasing ceramic particle size. Additionally, for equal sized pore, ceramic and conductor particles the TPB density shows an optimum near 1/3 occupation of each phase in the cell. Future opportunities for model development also are considered.

topic: Manufacturing and Characterization of Carbon Nanotube Microcable
title: Manufacturing and Characterization of Carbon Nanotube Microcable
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Timothy Ochmann
abstract: Carbon Nanotubes (CNTs) have gained attention over the past two decades because of their extraordinary strength and electrical properties. CNTs are a good candidate to replace copper wire for electric power distribution because of their corrosion resistance, low density, and high cycle fatigue. At the University of Cincinnati’s Nanoworld Labs, CNTs are grown on a silicon wafer substrate by a Chemical Vapor Deposition process. CNTs are then “spun” in a similar fashion as silk into a macroscopic thread (CNT thread). This CNT thread is about half the width of a human hair. The objective of the reported research efforts was to determine the most effective way to improve the electrical properties of CNT thread. Currently, the conductivity of “as spun” CNT thread is around three orders of magnitude lower than copper. By post treatments, we have been able to achieve conductivity of 105 S/m, which is about two orders of magnitude lower than that of copper. In addition, experiments have been conducted to coat the CNT thread with a polymer making its surface insulating as that of a metal electric cable. We expect further improvement in the electrical conductivity of CNT thread which will allow using it in electromagnetic devices, thus replacing copper wire and reducing the weight of the devices.

title: Exploring Hydrophobicity in Halogen-Substituted EDOT Films

authors_text: Gavin J. Donley, Joseph A. Adreani, Kenneth L. Brown and Elizabeth M. Sanford
abstract: Three new monomers of 3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene (EDOT) were synthesized and tested for electropolymerization feasibility. The organic moiety attached to the EDOT unit contained a fluorinated, chlorinated, or unsubstituted phenol ring The monomers were electropolymerized onto both glassy carbon and ITO surfaces. The polymer coatings were characterized in supporting electrolyte solutions of dichloromethane and water using cyclic voltammetry. Other methods such as atomic force microscopy (AFM), ellipsometry, and contact angle measurements were also used to characterize the polymer coatings. Cyclic voltammetric studies and contact angle measurements indicate that the fluorinated compound produces a hydrophobic film, while the film from the phenolated compound showed less hydrophobicity. From initial results, the chlorinated compound appears to be more similar to the fluorinated monomer than the phenolated compound.

abstract: The development of electrochemical sensors capable of detecting heavy metals is of benefit to the fields of environmental chemistry and environmental restoration. Development of an electrochemical sensor for heavy metals can be accomplished through preparation of a monomer that can simultaneously form a stable electrode coating and contain functionality to detect heavy metals. This poster describes the preparation of a monomer containing the polymerizable compound 3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene (EDOT) with a heavy metal sensing ligand, boron-dipyrromethene (BODIPY). Synthetic routes to two different BODIPY functionalized EDOT’s are described. One has a short link between the two moieties while the other has a four carbon alkyl chain spacer. The compounds were electrochemically polymerized and the resultant electrode films characterized via cyclic voltammetry.

topic: Study of n-Heptane Diffusion through Fire Fighting Foams As a Function of Temperature
title: Study of n-Heptane Diffusion through Fire Fighting Foams As a Function of Temperature
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Katherine Campbell and Bradley Williams
abstract: Study of n-Heptane Diffusion through Firefighting Foams as a Function of Temperature Katherine Campbell* and Bradley Williams Code 6185, Combustion Dynamics and Modeling Section Chemistry Division, Naval Research Laboratory, Washington DC 20375 *Naval Research Enterprise Intern, June-August 2013 Aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) is used to combat fires above pools of liquid fuel. AFFF was originally developed to provide fire protection on aircraft carrier flight decks, and has been widely used in both military and civilian applications (for example, airports) for some 50 years. AFFF and other types of firefighting foam are typically packaged as 1%, 3%, or 6% concentrates. The number refers to the percentage of the concentrate when mixed with water to form a solution. The concentrate contains surfactants and other additives that promote foam formation and stability. AFFF used for fire protection in the Department of Defense must pass the MIL-F-24385F qualification standard, which requires extinguishment of a 6 foot diameter pool fire of gasoline within 30 seconds when an AFFF solution is sprayed at a rate of 2 gallons/minute. Aqueous film forming foam relies on fluorinated surfactants to lower the surface tension of dense water and allow a film of the foam solution (10-50 µm) to form on top of the less dense fuel. This film can act as a barrier, even in the absence of foam, preventing the transport of fuel vapor from the pool to the flame above. The fluorosurfactants, however, pose as an environment concern due to persistence in the environment, and in some cases, tendency to bioaccumulate. Therefore, there is a desire to develop alternative firefighting foams free of environmentally-persistent materials. Achieving the same performance level as AFFF without fluorosurfactants requires more detailed understanding of the mechanisms by which fire suppression occurs. The present work investigates one aspect of foams’ interaction with the fuel pool: the mass transport of fuel through the foam layer. In particular, the diffusion of n-heptane is measured through an AFFF foam and a non-fluorinated (non-filming foam) at temperatures ranging from 16 °C to 50 °C. We examined two commercially available fire protection foams: Buckeye BFC-3MS (a MIL-F-24385F-qualified 3% AFFF) and Solberg RF6 (a 6% non-fluorinated foam qualified against the ICAO protocol). Foam was generated using a submerged sparger tube that bubbled nitrogen through the foam solution. Because this experiment focused on the mass transport effects of heated fuel, the foam generation conditions were kept constant by using a nitrogen flow rate that coincided with a foam expansion ratio between 9 and 10. n-Heptane was used as the fuel, selected as a pure compound representative of low flash point fuels. Heptane (mixed isomers) is used as the test fuel in some AFFF qualification standards, and is currently being investigated as a replacement test fuel in the MIL-F-24385F MilSpec AFFF standard, which currently uses gasoline. To observe fuel transport, we covered a heated pool of fuel in a 5.75 cm inner diameter chamber covered with a 4 cm layer of foam. The fuel was preheated before beginning the experiment, then the lower portion of the chamber was immersed in a temperature-regulated water bath. The fuel temperature was monitored by a thermocouple immersed in the fuel. We designed a test apparatus for this experiment to ensure that no fuel was in the chamber above the foam when testing began. This procedure established an initial condition of no fuel concentration within the foam layer; fuel leaving the top surface of the foam had to diffuse through the foam. Both the steady state flux of fuel through the foam and the time required for the fuel to penetrate the foam are proportional to the diffusivity of the fuel within the foam. We designed the test apparatus so that it could be quickly disassembled into two pieces. The lower half of the chamber contained the fuel pool, and when the chamber was disassembled, the foam layer was placed above the fuel before the chamber was reassembled. The top piece had nitrogen flowing through a porous frit toward the upper surface of the foam in a stagnation flow geometry. The nitrogen flow picks us any heptane which has diffused through the foam. The heptane concentration of the exiting as is determined by a Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometer; the heptane flux through the foam is calculated from the nitrogen flow rate, the heptane concentration, and the foam surface area. The chamber was designed for quick assembly to minimize the length of time between foam generation and the beginning of data collection (typically 1-2 minutes). We evaluated the two foams at fuel temperatures of 16 °C, 35 °C, and 50 °C. For each foam, two data collection runs were performed at 16 °C (ambient temperature) and three runs at each of the elevated temperatures. Data collection for each run lasted for slightly more than 60 minutes, or until the foam layer collapsed to expose the fuel surface. For both foams tested, the fuel flux through the foam increased significantly with increasing temperature. However, the increase in vapor pressure of the fuel, representing the boundary condition at the bottom of the foam in contact with the fuel surface, accounted for almost all of the effect. The diffusivity of n-heptane through either foam had little variation over the temperature range studied. The RF6 had a significantly higher conductivity for heptane than did the BFC-3MS AFFF. Further observations with additional foam formulations are needed to determine if the difference in diffusion is due to the presence of fluorosurfactants, or other factors. The magnitude of heptane diffusivity through the foams is intermediate, on a logarithmic scale, between its diffusivity in gases and in liquids.

abstract: Core-shell structured polystyrene-gold composite particles are synthesized from one-step Pickering emulsion polymerization. The core-shell particle’s surface coverage of the gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) is improved with increasing AuNP hydrophobicity and concentration. At high surface coverage, the AuNPs exhibit an ordered hexagonal pattern likely due to electrostatic repulsion during the emulsion polymerization process. In addition to core-shell structured polystyrene-gold composite particles, an intriguing observation is that under low AuNP concentrations, asymmetric polystyrene-gold nanocomposite particles are simultaneously formed, where a single gold nanoparticle is attached onto each polystyrene particle. It is found that these asymmetric particles are formed via a “seeded-growth” mechanism. The core-shell and asymmetric polystyrene-gold composite particles prove to be efficient catalysts as they successfully catalyze the Rhodamine B reduction reaction with stable performance and show high recyclability as catalysts.

topic: Exploring Multiphase Viscous Drop Impact with a Bulk Fluid Interface
title: Exploring Multiphase Viscous Drop Impact with a Bulk Fluid Interface
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Alison N. Logia, Travis W. Walker and Gerald Fuller
abstract: Project Abstract: AIChE Regional and National 2013 250 word limit Exploring Multiphase Viscous Drop Impact with a Bulk Fluid Miscible fluid systems are all around us from the mixture of water and dish soap to the dissolution of oxygen into blood. Building our intuition about how miscible and immiscible fluid systems differ can significantly further our understanding of fluid mechanics. We have developed an experiment to explore how a droplet impacts a bulk fluid interface. A drop of dense, viscous fluid is ejected from a syringe, free falling into a bath of water. A high-speed video is captured by triggering a laser photo diode system. These liquid-liquid drop impact systems can be inherently complex due to the time dependent interfacial tension between the two phases. Their interactions can produce a variety of unique shapes and morphologies including toroids, liquid columns, and captured bubbles. We aim to understand the conditions under which these various regimes form and the physics governing their formation. One particularly interesting regime is the "free-surface pendant drop." Under certain conditions, drops will partially wet the bath surface, residing on top of the bath despite the drops greater density. Interfacial tension between the drop and the bath reduces, as the drop dissolves into the bath, and the drop is driven down into the bath once gravity overcomes the interfacial tension. Between the surface of the bath and the bulk of the downward driven drop, a liquid column is formed. The liquid columns formed by these "free-surface pendant drops," as well as many other regimes, could have a variety of practical applications in industry.

topic: Synthesis and Characterization of Curcumin Dimethacrylate to Synthesize Biodegradable Poly(B-Amino Ester) Antioxidant Polymers
title: Synthesis and Characterization of Curcumin Dimethacrylate to Synthesize Biodegradable Poly(B-Amino Ester) Antioxidant Polymers
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: William Kelley, Nihar Shah, Thomas Dziubla and Zach Hilt
abstract: Curcumin is a well-known antioxidant which has been shown to relieve oxidative stress and assist in the wound healing process. However, previous attempts to deliver curcumin as an antioxidant drug have met with limited success, due to the low bioavailability of curcmin and the rapid degradation of curcumin in the body. Therefore, it is desirable to convert curcumin to biodegradable poly(β-amino ester) (PBAE) polymers which would protect curcumin from this rapid degradation, and which could be applied directly to the wound site. The polymer would release curcumin as the polymer degrades, aiding in the wound healing process. We have previously synthesized PBAE polymers using curcumin diacrylate (CDA). However, given the high reactivity of acrylate groups to primary amines (Michael Addition reaction), polymerization was difficult to control, resulting in polymers with suboptimal physical characteristics and degradation properties. As the methacrylate functional group is typically less reactive than the acrylate analog, it is hypothesized that the polymerization rate can be better controlled by the use of curcumin dimethacrylate (CDMA) versus a diacrylate system. In this work, CDA and CDMA monomers were synthesized and subsequent polymers are compared qualitatively, visually, and via polymer degradation. We found that CDMA is much less reactive than CDA; so much so, that the CDMA-based PBAE hydrogels degrade much too rapidly, probably because of significantly lower crosslinking.

topic: Hydrogels for the Replacment of Spinal Discs
title: Hydrogels for the Replacment of Spinal Discs
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences

abstract: Hydrogels for the Replacement of Spinal Discs Wyatt Self, Marissa Thierheimer, Allison Lind, Gabby Fief, and Skip Rochefort Polymer Laboratory, School of Chemical, Biological, and Environmental Engineering Oregon State University Corvallis, OR 97331 Every year millions of people experience back pain. Back pain can be caused from a variety of sources, such as thinning, herniated, ruptured and compressed discs. The purpose of this project was to determine a suitable replacement for damaged spinal discs that could be injected directly into the spine. Current procedures are invasive and often leave the patient with pain or limited mobility. Finding a hydrogel which could be injected directly into the spine to replace the damaged nucleus pulposus would result in a less costly and possibly more effective solution. In order to evaluate a hydrogels potential for use in the spine two types of testing were performed. The first test was a dynamic oscillatory frequency test which changes the frequency at which a gel sample was being twisted while the amount it is twisted remains constant. An AR2000ex rheometer is used to complete this test. The second test was completed using a Bose ELF 3200. This test compressed the gel by lowering a plate onto the gel at a constant rate. The purpose of the frequency testing was to determine the viscous and elastic properties of the gel; compression testing finds the strain and stress that a gel can withstand. Based on the results of these tests, as well as qualitative findings, such as how the gel broke, we could determine which gels would be suitable for replacing spinal discs. In order to make these gel discs, powdered gel was added to 90°C water. When all added powdered was dissolved into the water, the liquid was injected into a mold and allowed to solidify. Each gel was 25 mm in diameter and approximately 5 mm thick to mimic the size of an adult spinal disc. Four different polymers were used to form these gels, including, Agarose, Kelcogel F, Kelcogel LT100 and Gelzan CM. To begin understanding the various properties of these gels, each gel was tested as the sole component of the hydrogel, using different weight percents to observe differences at lower and higher percentages. After running these pure samples it was determined that each gel had very unique properties that could be combined to improve the quality of a hydrogel. Agarose displayed a solid structure but was very brittle and handled compression poorly. Kelcogel F didn’t display any positive properties as it was soft and broke easily however, it could be added to Agarose to slightly improve Agarose’s brittle nature. Kelcogel LT100 was very different than the other gels mentioned. This gel was very elastic and would stretch greatly before breaking or tearing; unfortunately it wasn’t very structured and would slowly stop returning to its original shape. Gelzan CM proved that it had potential to be the only polymer in a hydrogel why still producing acceptable results. . It had a very high compression value and was much more resilient to tearing than the first two gels mentioned. With knowledge of these characteristics it was possible to begin testing combinations of multiple polymers. Gelzan wasn’t available when testing first began resulting in lower compression values during the first two weeks of testing. After several tests, it was determined that total weight percents should be between 2.75 and 3.5%; less than this range caused the gel to lack structure and fall apart easily however, higher than this range caused the hydrogel to become ridged, lacking flexibility. Combinations consisting of Gelzan CM and LT100 proved to be the most effective, offering extremely high breaking points and sufficiently high percent strain values at breaking. To further this research, dynamic compression testing would be beneficial to more closely compare hydrogels qualities to the stresses that a spine undergoes daily. Testing the properties of other hydrogels could also lead to advancements in this research.

topic: Strong Glycosaminoglycan Hydrogels for Tissue Engineering Applications
title: Strong Glycosaminoglycan Hydrogels for Tissue Engineering Applications
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Jason Schulteis, Anahita Khanlari and Stevin H. Gehrke
abstract: Hydrogels are hydrophilic materials that typically contain over 95% water and are widely used in tissue engineering and drug delivery applications. However, due to high water content, hydrogels are weak and brittle. Therefore, methods to improve their mechanical performance (especially moduli and fracture strain) are highly sought. For tissue engineering scaffolding purposes, glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), such as hyaluronic acid (HA) and chondroitin sulfate (CS) have been of great interest for hydrogels since they are biocompatible and abundant in the mammalian extracellular matrix. However, like many other hydrogels, GAG based hydrogels typically do not possess the mechanical properties that are needed for a mechanically robust tissue engineering scaffold. To address this problem, in this study functionalized (methacrylated) HA and CS were photo-copolymerized with acrylate oligomers of ethylene glycol. The hypothesis was that acrylate oligomers of ethylene glycol could improve the crosslink density of the copolymer gels by improving the reaction yield through bridging the macromere functional groups with the crosslinker and grow the kinetic chains, which otherwise due to steric limitations would not be possible. Methacrylated hyaluronic acid (MHA) was co-polymerized with acrylate ethylene glycol (EG) oligomers with lengths varying from (EG) 2 DA to (EG) 13 DA . It was found that as the lengths of the EG oligomers increased, the shear modulus, Young’s modulus, and crosslink density of the co-polymerized gels improved. When the crosslinker spacer length increased from (EG) 2 DA to (EG) 13 DA, the shear modulus increased from 191 kPa to 268 kPa while the Young’s modulus increased from 658 kPa to 949 kPa. The crosslink density was increased from 0.824 mol/cm 3 to 0.962 mol/cm 3 for (EG) 2 DA and (EG) 13 DA respectively. As buffer solutions are used in tissue engineering practices, the salt effect on swelling, moduli, and the crosslink density of these gels were studied. For this purpose, methacrylated chondroitin sulfate (MCS) was equilibrated in salt solutions of different ionic strengths (0.01M to 1.4M sodium chloride solutions). For a MCS 13 wt% gel, it was found that as the salt concentration increased, the swelling degree decreased from 42 to 8. Additionally, for the same range of salt concentration the shear modulus decreased from 47 kPa to 9 kPa and the Young’s modulus decreased from 141 kPa to 27 kPa. With increasing salt concentration, the crosslink density decreased from 0.256 mol/cm 3 to 0.0277 mol/cm 3 .

topic: Superhydrophobic Copper Foils Via Aqueous Ammonia Etching and Alkyltrichlorosilane Modification
title: Superhydrophobic Copper Foils Via Aqueous Ammonia Etching and Alkyltrichlorosilane Modification
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Jarrid Ristau
abstract: Using surface modification to generate unique properties on a variety of substrates has been a field of intense investigation in recent decades. One poster-child of this work has been the development of countless methods for achieving superhydrophobicity – that is, liquid contact angles in excess of 150° - on myriad substrates. However, this development has lagged for certain materials, such as engineering metals (copper, aluminum, etc.) and inorganic metal oxides, due to technical challenges associated with their high surface energies. In this work, a simple immersion method is presented as a route to superhydrophobicity on copper foils. The foil is cleaned ultrasonically and then etched in aqueous ammonia for 24-72 hours, allowing for evaporation of the etchant. Initially, oxygen adsorption corrosion drives the dissolution of copper. After some time, a copper hydroxide precipitate forms and slowly deposits as a patina layer on the copper surface. When evaporation is complete, the copper hydroxide coated foil is exposed to an alkyltrichlorosilane, and subsequently, water contact angles as high as 165º may be observed.

topic: Cavitation Rheology
title: Cavitation Rheology
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Deirdre Brockwell, Seyed Meysam Hashemnejad and Santanu Kundu
abstract: Cavitation rheology is the study of the mechanical behavior of gels and other soft solids upon the introduction of cavities. In this project we applied cavitation rheology to measure the elastic modulus of a triblock copolymer gel. Gels were obtained by dissolving 5% and 10% volumes of a triblock copolymer, poly(methyl methacrylate)–poly(n-butyl acrylate)–poly(methyl methacrylate), in 2 ethyl-1-hexanol. In these experiments a needle connected to a syringe was inserted in the gel. The air within the syringe was compressed at different rates, ranging from 0.1 to 5 mL/min, using an automated syringe pump, causing a buildup of pressure and leading to cavitation in the form of a rapidly growing bubble. The pressure at which the gel cavitates is called the critical pressure, and is related to the Young’s modulus, or elasticity, of the gel plus the surface tension between the gel and the air and the inverse of the size of the needle tip, which was varied by using needles of different diameters. Both the critical pressure and the size and nature of the bubble are being analyzed to investigate the mechanical behavior of these gel at any arbitrary locations within the material.

title: Linear-Low Polyethylene Nanocomposite Fabrication Via Solid-State/ Melt Extrusion

abstract: Linear-Low Polyethylene Nanocomposite Fabrication via Solid-State/ Melt Extrusion David A. Frey and Katsuyuki Wakabayashi Department of Chemical Engineering Bucknell University Lewisburg, PA 17837 Combining a commercial polymer with an advanced filler material can yield a composite with a range of enhanced properties. Nanocomposites have recently been of interest because the nano -scale of the filler can impart unique properties for very low loading percentage. The production of these nanocomposites has been accomplished through several methods, but the knowledge about their differences is limited. The most common method in industry is twin-screw extrusion (TSE). This method uses a heated extruder barrel to disperse the filler in a molten polymer matrix. In contrast to this method, solid-state shear pulverization (SSSP) uses a chilled barrel to produce nanocomposites . Shear and compressive forces pulverize and mix the two materials, yielding a powder product. A recently developed process, solid-state/ melt extrusion (SSME), attempts to combine the benefits of both previous processes and uses a barrel split between cold and hot sections. Due to the differences in nature of these processes, variations in the properties and performance of the resulting nanocomposite products are expected. TSE is able to hold high production output while SSSP attempts to produce the most consistent and physically enhanced product throughout its powder producing processing. SSME allows for an increase in production rate similar to TSE and emulates the pulverization section of the SSSP process. This study compares the TSE, SSSP, and SSME processing on several model linear low-density polyethylene-based nanocomposites. Various types of carbon-based fillers, namely graphite, carbon nanotubes, and carbon black, were employed as fillers to observe differences in the physical properties of the outputs. Mechanical properties were determined via tensile-testing, while degradation behavior was examined via thermogravimetric analysis. Interpreting these results leads to predictions about how different processing affects the morphology of nanocomposites.

title: Examining Cytoskeletal Organization and Cell Morphology on P(MEO2MA-co-OEGMA) Thermoresponsive Biomaterials of Variable Lower Critical Solution Temperature

authors_text: Allyson Hill and Lauren S. Anderson
abstract: Thermoresponsive polymer (TRP) substrates as in vitro cell culture platforms have recently gained popularity due to their ability to release cells from the growth substrate without biochemical enzymes and while maintaining cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions. Cells grown on TRPs are released from their culture surface by a simple change in temperature below the lower critical solution temperature (LCST) of the polymer. P(MEO2MA-co-OEGMA) substrates offer a unique advantage over PNIPAM, the gold standard: the ability to tune the LCST. In this work, we investigate cell growth on four P(MEO 2 MA-co-OEGMA) substrates of varying LCST using immunofluorescence and confocal microscopy. The effects of tunable LCST on cell adhesion was also investigated using contact angle as a proxy for cellular adhesion. Specifically, we quantified the equilibrium spreading coefficient of P(MEO 2 MA-co-OEGMA) thermobrushes with aqueous LCSTs of 28, 31, 34, and 37°C as a function of temperature and examined cell height and cytoskeletal organization over the course of 48 hours. Results show that surface hydrophobicity increases as LCST decreases, with LCST of 28 o C being the most hydrophobic surface. Phase contrast microscopy images revealed an increase in cell adhesion as a function of LCST, with the most hydrophobic surface (28 o C) promoting cell spreading comparable to a TCP control. Cell height also varied with changing LCST. In conclusion, thermoresponsive brushes synthesized from random copolymers of 2-(2-methoxyethoxy)ethyl methacrylate (MEO 2 MA) and oligo(ethylene glycol) methacrylate (OEGMA) (P(MEO 2 MA-co-OEGMA)) that exhibit variable aqueous LCST values can be used to promote cell adhesion in tissue engineering applications.

abstract: The dental industry has long been hindered by poor adhesion quality between the dentin and enamel with dental composite during restoration. The result of this is restorations being performed on teeth that have previously been restored, which causes a significant loss of tooth mass. A study of the effects of plasma treatment on the tooth-adhesive interface was conducted. Tensile strength tests on treated and untreated specimen indicate that plasma treatment has a noticeable effect on the strength of the adhesive. Wetting ability of the adhesive, tested qualitatively with contact angle data, indicates that plasma treatment plays a significant role in tooth surface energy and adhesive wetting ability. These results indicate that plasma treatment can potentially result in a stronger, longer lasting adhesive with less tooth loss.

topic: A Method for Clean H2 Generation from Solar Heat and Water
title: A Method for Clean H2 Generation from Solar Heat and Water

authors_text: Kayla Weston, Christopher L. Muhich, Darwin Arifin, Alan W Weimber and Anthony H. McDaniel
abstract: Solar thermal water splitting is a method to transform diffuse, temporal, solar energy into a useful chemical fuel, namely H 2 that can be stored, transported and efficiently used. Solar thermal water splitting occurs when a metal oxide, “hercynite” material in this study, is heated using solar thermal energy to above 1200 o C where by it reduces generating oxygen. Traditionally, the material is then cooled ~ 300-500 o C below the thermal reduction temperature and exposed to steam whereby the steam re-oxidizes the metal oxide and produces H 2 gas. The metal oxide is subsequently cycled between the oxidation and reduction steps resulting in an overall reaction of H 2 O + solar thermal energy → H 2 + ½O 2 . The “hercynite” material used experimentally was synthesized using atomic layer deposition (ALD). ALD is a thin film coating technique that allows for a layer-by-layer deposition of metal oxides at the desired ratios and thickness. Thin films with high porosity are desired as they allow for decreased diffusional and thermal resistances. We demonstrate water splitting cycles using “hercynite” active material where the oxidation and reduction steps are carried out under isothermal conditions and that this is beneficial from an efficiency, total hydrogen generation, and material thermal stress standpoint. Additionally, in collaboration with Sandia National Laboratories, a follow up investigation of isothermal solar thermochemical cycling was carried out in order to better understand the cycle capacity and hydrogen productivity of hercynite materials over a range of operating temperatures and reactive gas partial pressures.

abstract: Cerium-doped gadolinium aluminum garnet (GAG:Ce) can be used to improve the efficiency of white-light LEDs (light emitting diodes). The Rogers group has gained expertise in combustion synthesis of yttrium aluminum garnet doped with Ce and/or Eu, however the process procedure does not produce good quality, pure phase GAG. This project focused on developing a gel-combustion synthesis of GAG:Ce. Photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy, powder x-ray diffraction (XRD), and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were used to characterize the effects of processing conditions on the resulting materials’ properties. Fuel type, combustion temperature, annealing temperature and annealing time were investigated. XRD showed that nearly pure phase GAG was formed by using citric acid as the fuel, a combustion temperature of 500°C, and a 4.5 hour, 1100 °C anneal. The trends observed in our results are consistent with phase diagrams that indicate pure-phase GAG should be formed at 1200 °C and above. Material combusted at 400 °C and annealed for 14 hours at 1100 °C had the most intense PL emission but did not contain the most garnet phase of the materials produced. This observation indicates PL emission intensity depends on factors in addition to crystal phase. We investigated the effects of substituting host ions on GAG PL intensity. Yttrium was substituted for gadolinium, and gallium was substituted for aluminum in the GAG lattice. XRD and XPS analyses were used to interpret the trends in PL emission of these host-doped materials.

abstract: Behavior of Particles as Tunable Emulsion Stabilizers Institute: City College of New York Topic: Fuels, Petrochemicals, and Energy Student's Name: Jannatul Ferdaous Mentor's Name: Ilona Kretzschmar PhD Candidate's Name: Sepideh Razavi Abstract Emulsions exist in our daily lives as natural and manufactured systems. Emulsion stability or instability is a huge concern for the industrial branched of pharmaceuticals, personal care, and oil recovery. It is expected for every pharmaceutical and food emulsion to aspire utmost stability which will help maintain the product's quality and conduct over a certain period of time. Adjusting the stability of emulsions can contribute immensely in development of new materials, regulating chemical reactions and new separation mechanism. Our primary goal of this research is to investigate the effect of modified particles on emulsion stability, and how their role differentiates from that of a simple surfactant in an emulsion. One of our main objectives of this research is to prove our hypothesis that unmodified and modified particles are capable of increasing the stability of emulsions. This past summer, a PhD candidate, Sepideh Razavi, and I worked on understanding the characteristics of oil-in-water emulsions. We used hexadecane and dilute aqueous KNO3 solution (10-4 M) to make emulsions, which we then centrifuged to increase the speed of coalescence and separation of oil and water phases. The longer time and the stronger centrifugal force a sample of emulsion requires to separate, the more stable the emulsion is. We tried to produce the most stable emulsions possible without the addition of particles by varying one of the many parameters in each experiment. After a number of experimental trials, we have settled on a 1:1 of oil and water mixture and an emulsification time of 60s to produce the most stable emulsion possible without particles. Eventually we progressed to experimenting with unmodified silica (SiO2) particles. We have worked with three different sizes (250nm, 500nm, and 1um) of particles to compare the effect they have on emulsion stability. As we proposed in our hypothesis, the particles did enforce a greater stability on the emulsion which enabled us to separate the process of coalescence from creaming. This leads us to the conclusion that particles can be used to produce stable emulsion, which can be very beneficial for pharmaceuticals and personal care industries.

title: Large-Scale Nanofabrication of Stacked Nanosphere Lithography Metasurfaces

authors_text: Yousif Alsaid, Alex Nemiroski, Mathieu Gonidec, Yanina Shevchenko and George M. Whitesides
abstract: Metamaterials have the potential to yield flat lenses, diffraction-unlimited microscopes, and even invisibility cloaks. A metamaterial’s optical properties are governed by the spacing and alignment of small nanostructures embedded inside the material. These nanostructures, through electrical and magnetic coupling, may give rise to a negative index of refraction over a specific electromagnetic frequency – a phenomenon not found anywhere in nature. However, fabrication of theorized Negative Index Metamaterials (NIMs), and other novel structures, has been difficult due to the limitations of 3D nanofabrication. This study proposes a new technique that utilizes Nano-Sphere Lithography (NSL) and spin-coating to stack metasurfaces and create 3D metamaterials. The process was optimized for polystyrene films, 200nm thick, and 25nm thick gold nano-antennas. We demonstrate the stacking of up to 3 NSL-defined metasurfaces, with no indication of a physical limit to how many layers can be stacked. The technique, hence, makes it more feasible to fabricate novel 3D metamaterials while still maintaining the resolution and simple fabrication offered by NSL.

topic: Thermal Properties and Ultrafast Dynamics of Phase Change Materials
title: Thermal Properties and Ultrafast Dynamics of Phase Change Materials
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Ben Weems, Aaron Lindenberg and Michael Shu
abstract: Phase Change Materials (PCMs) are materials which can be repeatedly switched between two or more phases; one amorphous and one or more crystalline. With a growing interest in the applications of PCMs, especially for improved solid-state memory technology, it is becoming more important to gain a fundamental understanding of the dynamics of their switching in order to design materials with faster switching speeds. Our emphasis was on the kinetics of PCM samples as they are heated and the impact this heating has on their transmission. The two methods used to measure the temperature dependence were a pump-probe test and FTIR spectroscopy. The most significant result, found in both the pump-probe tests and the FTIR, was that transmission of the materials decreased as temperature increased. Long-term effects from heating were also witnessed. One millisecond after being struck by the pump beam and one hour after being heated to 65° C in the FTIR, the transmission had not yet returned to its original value. The future of this project focuses on altering the pump-probe measurement to ensure the witnessed effects are caused by thermal, not electrical, changes of the PCM. This will be accomplished by measuring the temperature jump induced by the pump and comparing it to the FTIR measurements and by decreasing the rep-rate of the pump to find a change in the long-term effects on transmission. With a better understanding of the kinetics of change in these materials, and the electric field-driven switching dynamics, we will be able to store our data reliably and compactly; vital characteristics of data storage in an increasingly mobile world.

These soft shelled devices are made using an elastomer gel with reinforced fibers. Two layers of gel of sealed together to create small air tight chambers. By pumping a fluid, such as air, into these chambers at low pressures, one would cause the chambers to expand. The fibers control the ways in which the devices bend when the fluid is pumped into the chambers. If one controls how these chambers expand and contract one could cause one of these robots to move around or even walk. The research goal is to cause this expansion of the gel to be caused be an electrical stimulation rather than the introduction of a fluid through a pump. This would allow for greater applications of these devices and make the mechanisms that work these devices to be much smaller. Research has shown that electrical stimulations can cause gels to expand and contract, by putting a controlled voltage through the device we hope to stimulate what occurred by pumping a fluid into one of the devices. Microfluidic devices were sent to the Geisinger Medical Center of Pennsylvania for use in cancer research. The devices are used by passing drugs or fluids through the channels. authors_text: Mikhail Grant
abstract: CIGS is a tetrahedrally-bonded semiconductor material that can be used in thin film photovoltaic cells. Particularly, it is a very promising and growing absorber technology for the p-type absorber layer of CIGS solar cells. On the other hand, the standard material used for the n-type buffer layer in CIGS solar cells is Cadmium sulfide (CdS). However, CdS is toxic and absorbs unwanted blue light and UV light. We would like to find a good alternative buffer layer as a possible replacement for CdS. Such buffer layers can be effectively deposited by thin film deposition technique called ALD. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is capable of depositing a variety of materials by gas-surface reaction methods. The motivation to use ALD to deposit n-type buffer layers is due the conformality of ALD-deposited films on rough films, as well as the uniformity in the resulting alloy composition both laterally and with regards to thickness. One buffer layer material that we have deposited via ALD on CIGS is Zinc Oxide (ZnO). Zno is used in channels called point contacts, which have been found to increase CIGS solar cell performance. To reduce the influence of interference recombination, one can passivate the p-n junction surface, except in a few places where one can create conductive channels with a transparent conductor (i.e. ZnO). Typically the conductivity of a buffer layer made of ZnO can be increased by 10-100 times when doped with Al. In our lab, we have been varying this Al:ZnO ratio, as well as the temperature of the ALD chamber to achieve lower resistivity values.

abstract: Lithium ion batteries are critical for renewable energy storage, but their charge capacity, cyclability, and energy and power densities need to be improved in order to meet the current energy storage demands. Silicon has the potential to meet many of these needs, but unfortunately it undergoes a large volumetric change when lithiated and delithiated. This work focused on fabricating a porous carbon thin film that will perfectly encapsulate a lithium silicide particle. When delithiation occurs, a void space will be left that perfectly accommodates the large volumetric changes of silicon the next lithiation step. We successfully fabricated several porous carbon thin films with and without lithium silicide. The most promising films have a composition of 95:5 weight percent polyacrylonitrile: pore former as 10 weight percent solids in dimethylformamide. Future work will be done to prevent the oxidation of lithium silicide. Once this is done, a battery can be built to test the new anode material.

topic: Organic Monolayers on p-Doped Silicon Affect Photocurrents of Photosystem I Films
title: Organic Monolayers on p-Doped Silicon Affect Photocurrents of Photosystem I Films
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Helena Keller, Siyuan Yang and G. Kane Jennings
abstract: Biohybrid solar cells convert light energy to electricity through the use of Photosystem I (PSI), a protein complex that drives photosynthesis in green plants. The near-one-hundred percent quantum efficiency of PSI, in addition to its vast abundance in nature, gives this technology enormous potential as a sustainable source of energy. Prior work from our group has shown that PSI films on p-doped silicon yield photocurrents that approach 1 mA/cm 2 , far exceeding those for unmodified silicon or for PSI on metals. In this project, we have investigated the use of organic monolayers deposited between the p-doped silicon semiconductor and the PSI layer to facilitate electron transfer and increase the stability of the PSI film. These monolayers were prepared by exposing silicon to solutions containing ω-terminated alkynes to produce an alkenyl attachment of the monolayer to silicon and create a surface of the ω-terminated functionality for interaction with PSI. Of the monolayer surface groups tested, including alcohols, amines, and carboxylic acids, the carboxylic acid terminus most consistently achieved the highest photocurrents, suggesting favorable electrostatic attraction between the negative surface of the monolayer and positive patches on PSI. Carboxylic acids of varying carbon chain lengths—specifically three, six, and seven carbons—were then tested using photochronoamperometry in order to observe the effect of monolayer thickness on photocurrent as well as the stability of the photocurrent over time. Differences in monolayer thickness did not have a noticeable impact on current, but all carboxylic acid-treated silicon samples retained over 60 percent more of their initial photocurrent density than the plain silicon control after 30 minutes of continuous testing.

title: Development of Antibody-Conjugated Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles for Biomedical Applications

abstract: Background: There is significant interest in antibody-conjugated Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles (MSNPs) due to their potential uses as drug/siRNA carriers, as well as imaging agents with enhanced detection limits. Current imaging techniques like immunofluorescence (IF) and flow cytometry methods require the use of a primary antibody and fluorescent secondary antibody and are known for having problems with photobleaching and imaging sensitivity. We believe that antibody-conjugated MSNPs are a promising alternative to both the primary and secondary antibody. For one, fluorescent MSNPs have been found to be more photostable than the fluorescent dye itself, and therefore less susceptible to photobleaching. These antibody-conjugated MSNPs may also aid in signal amplification, increasing their sensitivity for use in detecting low-abundance proteins in cells. Finally, antibody-conjugated MSNPs contain a variety of other valuable features including relative ease of synthesis, batch-to-batch reproducibility, modifiability, a large surface area relative to its size, and pores for drug/probe loading. Methods/Characterization: Our current synthesis procedure was divided into three distinct steps: 1) Micelle Template Formation, 2) Silica Condensation, and 3) Template Removal (by acidic reflux). After MSNP synthesis, DLS was used to measure the hydrodynamic size and charge of the MSNPs. Then, to functionalize the nanoparticles, the MSNPs were coated first with Polyethyleneimine (PEI) and then with Polyethylenegylcol (PEG) before conjugating an antibody targeting a given protein. We found that it was possible to modify the surface groups of the nanoparticles by introducing different silanes 15 minutes after TEOS co-condensation. These modifications included: using (3-Mercaptopropyl) trimethoxysilane to for thiol surface groups and (3-Aminopropyl) trimethoxysilane for amine surface groups. We tested for the presence of these groups using Ellman’s Reagent and Fluorescamine assays. This surface modification was utilized for direct conjugation of antibody to nanoparticles, having PEG as a spacer. BCA/microBCA assays were also used to characterize the loading amount of antibody on the nanoparticles. We conjugated our developed MSNP with Trastuzumab (Herceptin) -- an antibody targeting the Human Epidermal Growth Factor 2 (HER-2) protein. This nanoconstruct was in turn evaluated for application in breast cancer targeting and treatment in our lab. Results: On average, we found that the size of nanoparticles synthesized this way were 70nm in diameter. The MSNPs were also found to have a negative charge of approximately -23mV in water. Additionally, due to our low Polydispersity Index (PDI) values (~0.002), and monodispersed size distribution, our nanoparticles hold great potential for development as antibody probes or drug carriers. The application of these developed mesoporous silica nanoparticles is currently under extensive investigation in our lab.

Data show that Ko/w increases as a function of salt concentration and linearly as a function of increase in OEGMA content of polymer. abstract: The breath figures (BFs) patterning technique represents a simple, robust method for producing microstructured honeycomb-patterned porous polymer films. Nanoparticles can self-assemble by spontaneous adsorption onto the interfaces between the templating water droplets and the polymer solvent in order to achieve controlled micrometer and nanometer scale hierarchical structures. Amphiphilic “Janus” nanoparticles were expected to optimize the films with regards to nanoparticle enrichment in the pore walls as well as ordering degree of the honeycomb structures given their dual role as Pickering emulsion stabilizing agents and as highly effective solid surfactants, providing a significant improvement over what has been achieved using isotropic nanoparticles. Exposed surfaces of silica particles embedded in spherical wax structures (colloidosomes) were chemically modified to render half of the particle hydrophobic. A reliable method for producing optimal colloidosome coverage was established. Upon successful synthesis of amphiphilic Janus particles, most reliably confirmed by a two-phase interface test, they were employed in the BFs templating method for the first time, resulting in regular, porous films with uniform, high nanoparticle density. Characterization of the films’ morphologies will help draw conclusions on the interfacial behavior and self-assembly performance of the Janus particles, as well as the general mechanism of BFs structure formation.

topic: The Effect of Free Radical Inhibitor on the Sensitized Radiation Crosslinking and Thermal Processing Stabilization of Polyurethane Shape Memory Polymers
title: The Effect of Free Radical Inhibitor on the Sensitized Radiation Crosslinking and Thermal Processing Stabilization of Polyurethane Shape Memory Polymers

authors_text: Cameron Maher, Keith Hearon, Sarah Smith, Thomas Wilson and Duncan Maitland
abstract: The effects of free radical inhibitor on the electron beam crosslinking and thermal processing stabilization of novel radiation crosslinkable polyurethane shape memory polymers (SMPs) blended with acrylic radiation sensitizers have been determined. The polyurethane SMPs in this study possess novel processing capabilities. These SMP’s have the ability to be melted and processed into complex geometries as thermoplastics and then crosslinked using electron beam irradiation in a final curing step. This novel method is potentially much more cost effective and efficient than current methods when high throughput is desired. To increase the effectiveness of radiation crosslinking, the radiation sensitizer pentaerythritol triacrylate (PETA) was solution blended with thermoplastic polyurethane SMPs synthesized from 2-butene-1,4-diol and trimethylhexamethylene diisocyanate (TMHDI). Since thermoplastic melt processing methods such as injection molding are readily carried out at elevated temperatures, premature crosslinking due to sensitizer thermal instability is a significant processing concern. To overcome sensitizer thermal instability, free radical inhibitor can be added to provide thermal stabilization. However, free radical inhibitor can reduce the effectiveness of radiation crosslinking. In this study, we determined the inhibition effects of the inhibitor 1,4-benzoquinone (BQ) on thermal stabilization and radiation crosslinking of polyurethane SMPs solution blended with PETA. Sol/gel analysis of irradiated samples showed that free radical inhibitor at concentrations of 0-10,000 ppm had little to no inverse effects on gel fraction. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) showed a minor negative correlation between inhibitor composition and rubbery modulus. The study also showed inhibitor BQ was highly effective on the thermal stabilization of acrylic sensitizer PETA. The thermoplastic blends could be heated to 150 °C for up to 5 hours or to 125 °C for up to 24 hours if stabilized with 10,000 ppm BQ without undesired sensitizer reaction occurring. The blended samples could also be heated to 125 °C for up to 5 hours if stabilized with 1000 ppm BQ without reaction. We believe this study provides significant insight into methods for manipulation of the competing mechanisms of radiation crosslinking and thermal stabilization of radiation sensitizers, thereby facilitating further development of radiation crosslinkable thermoplastic SMPs.

abstract: Crystal Structure and Morphology of Adipic Acid/PVP Particles Formed via Monodisperse Droplet Evaporation Tara L. Panzarino Advisor: Ryan C. Snyder Bucknell University, Department of Chemical Engineering Particle characteristics and formation play a large role in the pharmaceutical industry. The characteristics of the particle determine the effectiveness and quality of the final drug product. In particular, the degree of crystallinity of the active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) can impact the dissolution and bioavailability of the API. Amorphous particles are desirable because they have higher solubility than any of the crystalline forms; however they are not always easy to produce. The goal of this work is to obtain amorphous particles of adipic acid, with the addition of an excipient. The resulting particles are compared to the morphology and crystallinity of particles formed only with adipic acid. In this work, the primary excipient considered is Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP). Particles of adipic acid and PVP are formed from the evaporation of monodisperse droplets produced from a Vibrating Orifice Aerosol Generator (VOAG). The VOAG creates monodispersed particles by applying a constant frequency across a solution jet to create droplets. These droplets are then allowed to dry in a column, and the particles can be collected and analyzed. Solutions of varying weight % ratios of adipic acid and PVP in isopropanol were considered. Particles of Adipic Acid and PVP were analyzed for structure using X-ray Diffraction. The results show that as the ratio of Adipic Acid to PVP became smaller, the particles became less crystalline in nature, with a transition around 50 weight % of each component. Morphology is also analyzed with SEM imaging. The morphology changes such that as the weight % ratio of Adipic Acid decreased, the particles became increasingly smooth. Adipic Acid particles ran through the VOAG in solutions of isopropanol typically have a wrinkled appearance, with a hole somewhere on the particle. Future plans also are presented.

title: Surfactant Removal from Single-Wall Carbon Nanotube Dispersions
