abstract: Until recently, the use of single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) in nanoelectronic devices has been limited due to the presence of both metallic and semiconducting SWCNT electronic-types. Advances in post-synthesis processing, using techniques such as column chromatography and density gradient ultracentrifugation (DGU), has allowed for successful SWCNT separation. Many separation techniques rely on the use of surfactants, commonly sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), to exploit differences in the surface chemistry or buoyant density of the SWCNTs, respectively. Therefore, complete surfactant removal from the SWCNT species is critical in order to fully probe the intrinsic physical and electrical properties of the electronic-type-separated SWCNTs. In the current study, an approach to surfactant removal is described whereby purification was systematically examined by employing a variety of acids, bases, and organic solvents. Upon mixing of the desired reagent, the SWCNT dispersions were bath sonicated, immersed in an ice bath, and observed over the course of 24 hours. Reagents were qualitatively deemed successful if they interrupted the SWCNT/surfactant interaction, yet did not change the solubility of the surfactant. Of those examined, five reagents yielded optimal results, including acetone, acetonitrile, N,N-dimethylacetamide, cyclohexylpyrrolidine, and ethanol. The SWCNTs were filtered into bulk papers, each containing 1 mg of SWCNT material, which was followed by thermal oxidation in air. Purification temperatures were determined based on the decomposition profile of the as-produced SWCNT paper obtained by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The purity of the treated SWCNT samples was characterized via Raman spectroscopy, optical absorbance spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and TGA. The use of organic reagents has led to a method for surfactant removal that also reduces filtration time, which may prove useful in large scale batch processing. Results demonstrating the successful removal of SDS from SWCNT dispersions will be discussed and compared to prevalent strategies previously reported in the literature.

abstract: Novel Block Copolymers as Proton Exchange Membranes for Fuel Cells and Specialty Separation Applications Efficient proton exchange membranes are the crucial component for fuel cells that could power the next generation of green energy devices. The industry standard to make these membranes is Nafion®, which although it has an excellent proton exchange capacity and great thermal stability, it can be expensive to mass produce and it has some mass-transfer limitations. Our goal is to make proton exchange membranes better to Nafion®’s properties with lower costs to produce. In this study, three inexpensive monomers were used to build the polymer chain: isobutylene, styrene and methyl vinyl ether. With a combination of these monomers block copolymers were synthesized and tested their properties with various materials characterization methods. Also, other combinations of polymers such as Poly(styrene-isobutylene-styrene) (SIBS) and Poly(styrene-isoprene-styrene) (SIS) were blended to test their properties. Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA) shows how the initiator for the Atom Transfer Radical Polymerization (ATRP) affects the overall degradation temperature of the polymer. Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) tests verify how 4-chlorobenzophenone initiated polymerizations that possess a lower melting point compared to the (2-chloroethyl)benzene samples. Also, the synthesized polymer chains show an expected increase in their number average molecular weight (Mn) and change in polydispersity (PD). Polymer blends with SIS and SIBS show different properties in permeability and water swelling tests that can imply that the right blend composition can cause synergistic results with the desired properties, which can be the next step for the Poly(isobutylene styrene methyl vinyl ether) (PIB-PS-PE) synthesized polymer to be blended with premade SIS and SIBS.

topic: Crystallization Kinetics of Polylactic Acid (PLA) Processed through Solid-State/Melt Extrusion
title: Crystallization Kinetics of Polylactic Acid (PLA) Processed through Solid-State/Melt Extrusion
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Brian Lynch
abstract: Polylactic acid (PLA) is a bio-based polymer derived from corn, sugar beets, and other natural sources. It has recently become of interest because of its biodegradability and similarity in properties to other petroleum-based polymers. However, the widespread use of PLA is currently hindered by its inherently slow crystallization kinetics relative to other commercial polymers. The desired semi-crystalline structure is difficult to achieve in a reasonable amount of time when extrusion and other melt-molding techniques are used. Many different methods have been attempted in enhancing the crystallization kinetics of PLA. One of the most prominent is nucleating agents. While effective, this method is not environmentally friendly and can be very costly. An alternative is processing via solid-state shear pulverization (SSSP), a method developed by Northwestern University. SSSP has been shown to lead to faster crystallization kinetics in both PLA and polyethylene terephthalate (PETE) without any additives or blend components. We have recently developed a related extrusion technique called solid-state/melt extrusion (SSME). SSME combines traditional twin-screw extrusion (TSE) and SSSP. SSME is designed to combine the advantages of these two processes in an attempt to increase the rate of crystallization for faster, more productive processing. So far, SSME has been shown to be an effective processing method for polypropylene and polyethylene blends. This study explores the crystallization behavior and physical properties of PLA processed via SSME. The effectiveness of processing was assessed by comparing the properties of SSME-processed samples to those of TSE and SSSP. The rate and level of crystallization was measured by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), while degradation behavior and mechanical properties were analyzed via thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and tensile testing, respectively.

topic: Analyzing ROS Generation From Magnetic Nanoparticles In An Alternating Magnetic Field and Its Role In Intracellular Hyperthermia
title: Analyzing ROS Generation From Magnetic Nanoparticles In An Alternating Magnetic Field and Its Role In Intracellular Hyperthermia
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Catherine E. Oliver, Robert J. Wydra, David B. Cochran, Kimberly W. Anderson, Thomas D. Dziubla and J. Zach Hilt
abstract: Through Brownian relaxation and Neel relaxation, magnetic nanoparticles are capable of absorbing energy from an alternating magnetic field (AMF) and converting it to heat. Thus, via passive targeting, nanoparticles can collect at the tumor site and by the application of an AMF provide localized heating throughout the tumor. Furthermore, internalized targeted nanoparticles have been recently shown to induce cellular death when exposed to an AMF without a measurable temperature rise, therefore stimulating great interest to develop targeted nanoparticles for the treatment of metastatic cancer via intracellular hyperthermia. Focusing on the iron oxide magnetic nanoparticle system, it is thought that at the molecular level a significant contributing factor to the iron oxide toxicity in intracellular hyperthermia is the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) through the Fenton and Haber Weiss reactions. This research, in turn, focuses on the effects of an AMF on the surface mediated production of ROS based on the hypothesis that these effects are a key contributor to the toxicity demonstrated as intracellular hyperthermia. Despite variance in temperature ranging 37-39°C, it was observed via the methylene blue dye degradation method that samples exposed to an AMF experienced increased ROS production. Moreover, the Arrhenius equation , , where s -1 and J, was determined from a series of kinetic studies. This equation showed that despite variability in heating profile, experimental values of dye degradation were consistently lower than the theoretical values indicating improved kinetics due to AMF exposure. Furthermore, AMF data points did not fit the derived Arrhenius trendline strongly suggesting that AMF mediated heating possesses a kinetic effect unique to that of bulk heating. Preliminary cell culture studies conducted by means of the viability-ROS assay suggested that as uncoated iron oxide magnetic nanoparticle concentration increases, ROS generation increases and cell viability decreases.

abstract: Bismuth telluride is a commonly-used thermoelectric material. In an effort to the increase its thermoelectric power (i.e., Seebeck coefficient), ionic liquids can be used to intercalate and exfoliate the bismuth telluride into two-dimensional nanosheets. The interaction parameter between bismuth telluride and the ionic liquid is important to determine a liquid that can intercalate easily into the Van der Waals gaps of bismuth telluride. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used to characterize the crystal faces and to calculate intercalated Van der Waals gaps. This interaction can then be used to determine suitable ionic liquid for bismuth telluride exfoliation.

topic: Self-Assembly Of Single Stranded DNA and Gold Nanoparticles
title: Self-Assembly Of Single Stranded DNA and Gold Nanoparticles
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Tasha Tucker
abstract: The unique properties of gold nanoparticles are utilized in a range of applications such as sensors, catalysis and drug delivery. Gold nanoparticles are often functionalized with ligands to prevent aggregation and control nanoparticle binding. Previous work in our group has shown that nanoparticles with positively charged ligands have the ability to wrap double stranded DNA (dsDNA) above a critical charge density. The interaction of dsDNA with AuNPs is dependent on parameters such as charge and polarity of attached ligands. Positively charged ligands are able to wrap DNA, while polar ligands cause less distortion in the DNA helix. Herein, we describe the use of molecular dynamics simulations to study the interactions of a random sequence of single stranded DNA (ssDNA) with varying ligands.We vary charge and polarity of ligand end groups by studying methyl (CH3), amine (NH2) and ammonia (NH3)modified ligands. Because ssDNA is much more flexible than dsDNA, we find a greater degree of wrapping for all particles. However, ssDNA is more compactly wrapped around gold nanoparticles with positively charged ligands (NH3) than with the CH3 and the NH2 end groups.

topic: Vertical Graphene By Plasma Enhanced Chemical Vapor Deposition: Correlation of Plasma Conditions and Growth Characterstics
title: Vertical Graphene By Plasma Enhanced Chemical Vapor Deposition: Correlation of Plasma Conditions and Growth Characterstics
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: David O'Brien, Emil Sandoz-Rosado, William Page, Joshua Przepioski, Dennis Mo, Benjamin Wang, Tam-Triet Ngo-Duc, Jovi Gacusan, Michael Winter, Robert Cormia, Shuhei Takahashi, M. Meyyappan and Michael Oye
abstract: Vertically aligned graphene was grown by plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition using methane feedstock. Optical emission spectroscopy (OES) was used to monitor the plasma species and Raman spectroscopy was used for characterizing the properties of as-grown, vertically-aligned graphene. OES-derived information on plasma species such as C, C 2 , CH, and H are correlated with the properties of the vertically-aligned graphene. Graphene grown at 250 W and 15 sccm exhibited the lowest amount of defects. While OES peak intensities occurred at the highest power and lowest flow conditions, the OES peak ratios of plasma species had a greater dependence on flow rate and exhibited a saddle point in the atomic C/H ratio corresponding to optimal growth involving the lowest amount of overall defects. Plasma diagnostics provide a valuable approach to optimize growth characteristics and material properties.

topic: Fluorescence and Gelation Properties of Cyanostilbene Derivatives
title: Fluorescence and Gelation Properties of Cyanostilbene Derivatives
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Nathan Mickinac, Yao Ma and Shimei Jiang
abstract: Molecules containing cyanostilbene have attracted interest for their variable fluorescence properties attributable to its cis-trans isomerization. Previous research has shown that synthesized V-shaped cyanostilbene amide derivative containing a tert -butyl group have gelation capability in a variety of solvents 1 . The purpose of this project was to synthesize and explore the gelation and fluorescence properties of V-shaped cyanostilbene amide derivatives containing alkoxy groups. The starting material for this synthesis, 5-hydroxyisophthalic acid, has a substitution of the hydroxyl group for an alkoxy group. The two carboxylic acids were reacted with a cyanostilbene amine to result in the desired product. The synthesis of a derivative containing a butoxy group was successful; however, exploration of alternate syntheses resulted in another molecule that has shown gelation properties in water that exhibits a transition temperature between gel and solution. The presence of water, acetonitrile, or methanol can influence the fluorescence of the solid to emit a green, blue, or yellow color, respectively. This molecule exhibits several characteristics that require further exploration. With additional research, such derivatives could be applicable as a separation basis between organic and aqueous phases as well as use in sensory applications. title: Formation of a 3-D Network in Alginate Spheres

authors_text: Paula Pacurari and Robin Hissam
abstract: FORMATION OF A 3-D NETWORK IN ALGINATE SPHERES West Virginia University, Department of Chemical Engineering Paula Pacurari, Dr. Robin Hissam A current challenge in the study of cancer is the development of 3D models for cell growth. Growth of cells on flat surfaces may not allow for proper signaling or migration, yielding results that may not mimic the actual behavior of cancer cells in vivo. With a focus on leukemia, a material that will mimic the bone marrow microenvironment can serve as a new model for the study of leukemic stem cells. Alginate is an immunocompatible biopolymer that is capable of immobilizing viable cells and bioactive factors and is a common biological material used in drug delivery and biomaterial applications. Upon the addition of CaCl 2, alginate forms a hydrogel which can be modified into different 3-D structures. The bone marrow microenvironment is highly porous, and this project was to develop alginate structures that mimic the bone marrow microenvironment and can be used as a 3-D model. Alginate beads were formed using different solution concentrations to create materials of varying microstructures. Swelling ratio tests were performed to determine the porosity and diffusion rate of fluid into the material. In addition, the morphology of the beads was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were be used to characterize the structure of the 3-D networks. The bead structures were also compared to a bulk gel structure, which indicates the production of beads results in more porosity on the surface.

abstract: Cochineal is a natural red dye extracted from an insect, and used worldwide as a textile and fabric dye. It an ideal red dye due to its brilliant carmine color, color strength and its colorfastness on many fabrics 1 . The dye permanently adheres to the fabric in the presence of a mordant - a metallic ion that forms a coordination complex with the dye and attaches it to the fabric. Larger concentrations of mordant have been shown to improve colorfastness 2 , but the thermodynamics of the process have not been investigated. In this project, we studied the thermodynamics of cochineal dye adsorption on wool fabric. Three mordants were selected: tin, alum, and copper. Four different adsorption isotherm models were fit to the data: Langmuir, Freundlich, Redlich-Peterson, and Temkin models. Initial results show that the Langmuir, Freundlich, and Temkin models fit the data. As more data is collected, we will determine the effect of mordant on the model parameters. topic: Selective Patterning of Bi2Te3 Nanoplatelets Via Microcontact Printing
title: Selective Patterning of Bi2Te3 Nanoplatelets Via Microcontact Printing
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Amira Aglan, Lingling Guo and Hung-Ta Wang
abstract: Bismuth Telluride (Bi 2 Te 3 ) and its family chalcogenides are recently confirmed as topological insulators. Their electrical transport is dissipationless, which will have an impact on future applications, including thermoelectrics, electronics, and IR detectors. One of the critical challenges is to selectively assemble two-dimensional Bi 2 Te 3 nanosheets on a variety of substrates. In this work, the chemistry of selectively patterning Bi 2 Te 3 nanoplatelets on silicon substrates using micro contact printing (μCP) technique is investigated. Masters of three μCP stamps (patterns of letter A, houndstooth and square array, respectively) were made using regular photolithography processes, and μCP stamps were fabricated by pouring polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) on the master and curing PDMS at a temperature of 65⁰C for 3 hrs. μCP processes were applied to print 3-Aminopropyltrimethoxysilane (APTMS) with the three designed patterns onto silicon substrates, and Bi 2 Te 3 nanoplatelets, grown via a solvo-thermal process, were coated selectively. The results indicate that Bi 2 Te 3 nanoplatelets are immobilized on the APTMS printed regions. It is suspected that an electrostatic interaction between positively-charged amine groups and negatively-charged Bi 2 Te 3 nanoplatelets is the driving force of the selective patterning. We have demonstrated that μCP is a controllable, facile process for assembling two-dimensional Bi 2 Te 3 nanosheets and other chalcogenides.

topic: Time-Evolved Characterization and Performance of Slips (Slippery Liquid-Infused Porous Surface) Tubing With Potential Drag Reduction
title: Time-Evolved Characterization and Performance of Slips (Slippery Liquid-Infused Porous Surface) Tubing With Potential Drag Reduction
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Derek Sun, Noah MacCallum, Philseok Kim, Mughees Khan and Joanna Aizenberg
abstract: The development of energy-efficient, low-drag fluid transport systems would have a substantial impact on many promising industrial and commercial applications including fire-fighting operations, irrigation systems, pipeline transport, district heating systems, marine vessels, turbo machines, sports gear, and next-generation biomedical apparatus. The potential for traditional superhydrophobic surfaces to address this need is severely limited by high-pressure instability, a weakness that is exacerbated when subjected to low surface tension flow medium. Wong et al. have recently introduced Slippery Liquid-Infused Porous Surfaces (SLIPS), a pressure-stable and truly omniphobic approach that promises to overcome these issues. Herein we rationally evaluate the viability of SLIPS as a means of drag reduction for fluid transport through metal pipes. We applied this functionalization, Slippery Liquid-Infused Porous Inner Pipeline Extruded Surfaces (SLIPIPES), to 3 mm ID aluminum pipes, characterized the system for longevity and, and observed effects on pressure drop. We used water as a flow medium to assess longevity and compare friction factor of untreated aluminum (untreated-Al), boehmitized-fluorinated aluminum (BF-Al), and SLIPS aluminum tubing (SLIPS-Al) as a function time. First, to gauge the longevity of various lubricants, we studied the SLIPIPES as a function of time and Reynolds number, with the lubricant retention and resultant slip characteristics monitored by weight changes and sliding angle of a water droplet, respectively. The lubricant layer depletes over time at a rate proportional to the thickness and viscosity of the lubricant layer and the shear rate of the flowing medium. We observe a transition in thinning rate from the excess layer to the bound, ‘critical’ layer, and the lubricant layer is depleted after 30 minutes for nominal flow rates. Lastly, we observe no significant drag reduction in turbulent regime as the increasing drag caused by lubricant shedding outweighs the inner surface roughness improvement by SLIPS.

topic: Integrated Opv-Otft System for Self-Powered, Solution Processable Organic Electronics
title: Integrated Opv-Otft System for Self-Powered, Solution Processable Organic Electronics
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Renata Hanna, Yan Zhou and Zhenan Bao
abstract: Abstract: Integrated OPV-OTFT System for Self-Powered, Solution Processable Organic Electronics Renata Hanna, Doctor Yan Zhou, Professor Zhenan Bao Bao Group, Department of Chemical Engineering, Stanford University The field of organic electronics has attracted much attention from academia and industry for its flexible, light, low-cost, and solution processable devices. In recent years, efficient organic photovoltaics (OPVs), organic diodes (OLEDs), and organic transistors (OTFTs) have been studied and optimized. Going beyond the development of individual devices, in our study we propose a more complex circuit integrating OTFTs and OPVs. Transistors are widely employed as amplifiers and control units in current devices. In TFTs, the gate serves as a control and the channel is responsible for the amplified response. In OTFTs, the channel is a thin-film of organic semiconductors. Photovoltaics (PV) are a promising technology for attending global energy challenges. In PVs, the active layer is composed by an electron donor component and an electron acceptor component and is responsible for absorbing light and converting it into electricity. In OPVs, the active layer is a film composed of a blend of organic semiconductors. The integrated circuit (IC) we propose moves away from individual devices and towards fully organic, complex circuitry that can be processed on a single substrate without the need for lithography, a limiting factor in inorganic electronics. In the IC, OPV cells generate the voltage potential necessary to drive the OTFT in the saturation region, in which the transistor achieves best amplification conditions. The circuit structure developed is solution processable, and could be applied onto flexible substrates for specific applications. In this way, the IC proposed is a self-powered, solution processable, low-cost, and potentially flexible organic system. The proposed structure was developed with the intent to enable OPV characterization under solution environments, which is required for the study of many applications of the technology. Besides the original intent, further applications have also been devised for the proposed system. One simple application would be to apply it to flexible and portable devices that require low-weight and independent power generation. Another application would be to combine the already proposed structure to more OFET devices such as to create what are called current mirrors, through which it would be possible to amplify the current depending on the relations between device sizes. A further application of this structure would be as a type of photodetector for what is known as smart windows, which change coloration and the amount of light passing through depending on the intensity of the incident light. These applications would require further inquiry, but seem reasonable with further study, optimization, testing, and data collection. Another application that would have great market impact would be the use of this structure, coupled with other circuit elements, as an alternative form of radio-frequency identification (RFID) active transmitter. This configuration is advantageous over other forms of RFID transmitters for several reasons, and currently, the most apparent is that it is less costly in terms of materials and production methods, since organic electronics require cheap materials that can be processed without the high temperatures and vacuum levels that inorganic electronics require. The integrated circuit was prepared from solution through spin-coating techniques. The integration was achieved through a complex planning such that the production steps did not conflict with one another. This is important with the preparation of layers through spin-coating because the solution that is the precursor to a following layer cannot be able to dissolve previously formed layers. Moreover, it is important to have layer-planning such that the steps taken between layer- deposition steps , such as curing and annealing, do not conflict with the needs of other layers. The development of the correct sequence of layering and processing revealed the need for further study of the thickness of the dielectric layer. Optimization of the solvent and concentration of the dielectric solution was necessary for the formation of a clear solution and of a proper thin-film with reduced number of defects and pin-holes. Moreover, the study of the influence of the concentration over the thickness of the layer indicated a possible trade-off between high mobilities and low threshold voltages. Lower dielectric solution concentrations yielded thinner layers with higher mobilities (µ) and threshold voltages (V TH ), under the condition that the layers were thick enough to prevent shunting due to pin-holes. In opposition to these results, more concentrated solutions yielded lower mobilities and threshold voltages. Consequently, there is a need for compromising between high mobilities and low threshold voltage, both of which are desirable characteristics for the proposed IC. Low threshold voltages are essential so that the OPVs are capable of driving the OTFTs, whereas high mobilities are more desirable because they ensure better device performances. The study of polymer blends for the OPV active layer indicated the need for further optimization of the threshold voltage of the OTFTs since on average the OPVs could only drive up to approximately 0.9V. Considering the IC structure, higher driving voltages would allow better performances and amplification capabilities for the transistors. Therefore, although this study has achieved an efficient process for the preparation of the IC, much needs to be done in order for the system to be operational. The main points that continue to be studied are the optimization of the dielectric layer of the OTFT and of the active layer of the OPV.

topic: Improvement of Cochlear Implants By Controlling and Quantifying Material Properties for Directing Neurite Growth
title: Improvement of Cochlear Implants By Controlling and Quantifying Material Properties for Directing Neurite Growth
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Austin Hangartner, Brad Tuft and Allan Guymon
abstract: One cause of deafness is the loss of hair cells within the cochlea. This particular type of deafness can be partially remedied with a cochlear implant. Although these implants can reproduce the basic sensation of hearing, they deliver little tonal information due to poor spatial resolution. The distance between the transmitting electrode and the receiving hearing elements allows the signal to spread and electrically stimulate multiple regions of the nerve cells within the cochlea. One solution to deal with the poor spatial resolution may be to regenerate and guide spiral ganglion neurites to decrease the distance or even contact the electrode. Accordingly, we use photopolymerization to synthesize materials with surface physical and mechanical cues to orient the growth of regenerative neurites. Mechanical properties ware controlled by varying cross linking density in hexyl methyl methacrylate (HMA) with 1,6 hexanediol dimethacrylate (HDDMA) and polyethylene glycol dimethacrylate (PEGDMA) with ethylene glycol dimethacrylate (EGDMA) co-polymers. Each co-polymer system can be controlled by varying each components concentration to manipulate the elastic modulus while maintaining a relatively constant surface polarity.

topic: Crystallographic Changes in Lead Zirconate Titanate Due to Neutron Radiation Exposure
title: Crystallographic Changes in Lead Zirconate Titanate Due to Neutron Radiation Exposure
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Alexandra J. Henriques, Jacob L. Jones, Jennifer S. Forrester, Joseph T. Graham, Sheldon Landsberger, Jon F. Ihlefeld, Geoffrey L. Brennecka and Donald Brown
abstract: Piezoelectric and ferroelectric materials are useful as the active element in non-destructive monitoring devices for high-radiation environments. However, such use requires knowledge of the structural response in the material to radiation exposure, and the nature of these changes is not currently known. Thus, the present work evaluates the change in the structure of a variety of technologically significant lead zirconate titanate (PZT) compositions. PZT based materials with a 50/50 zirconium to titanium ratio of the following three compositions were investigated: (1) undoped, (2) Fe-doped, and (3) Nb-doped PZT. Powder samples and disc shaped samples of all three compositions were synthesized using solid state processing. Laboratory X-Ray diffraction was used to determine the initial phase purity of the materials. topic: Influence of Catalyst Deposition on Charge Carrier Trapping at Catalyst-Semiconductor Interfaces
title: Influence of Catalyst Deposition on Charge Carrier Trapping at Catalyst-Semiconductor Interfaces
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Steven Chavez and Ian Sharp
abstract: The production of solar fuels via photoelectrochemical water splitting is an attractive option for satisfying the world’s demand for clean energy. The success of this solar-to-chemical energy conversion depends highly on the identification of a stable and efficient photoanode for water oxidation. Bismuth vanadate (BiVO 4 ) is a promising photoanode material because of its small band gap, its stability over large pH ranges and favorable location of its valence band edge relative to the water oxidation potential. However, its surface is not catalytically active for water oxidation and its performance is limited. This problem can be mediated by the integration of an effective water oxidation catalyst such as cobalt phosphate (Co-Pi). Nevertheless, defects created at catalyst-semiconductor interfaces can lead to charge carrier trapping, preventing charge transfer to the catalyst and lowering conversion efficiency. This work provides a quantitative analysis of the accumulation of photogenerated holes at catalyst-semiconductor interfaces as a function of semiconductor doping and electrocatalyst deposition. In situ transient photocurrent and photovoltage behavior of a BiVO 4 photoanode coated with a Co-Pi electrocatalyst were measured in both a standard aqueous electrolyte and in one containing a sacrificial reagent. Associated time constants were analyzed to determine deleterious carrier trapping at these interfaces. Comparisons were also made with nominally undoped BiVO 4 , and molybdenum doped BiVO 4 with and without catalyst. Results presented here provide an important step to identifying parameters affecting the quality of BiVO 4 /Co-Pi interface and solidify a method of analyzing similar types of interfaces of importance to the development of artificial photosynthesis.

Ideally, the ceria film should exhibit smooth surface morphology, high bulk crystallinity, and low surface impurity levels. Films were grown under a variety of conditions, from substrate cleaning methods to film annealing conditions. The results illustrate that the doping, PLD target processing parameters, and substrate crystal orientation have the greatest impact on the ceria film surface characteristics.

In this study, the production of poly(lactic acid) (PLA) nanoparticles is investigated using solvent displacement in a batch fed continuous impingement jet mixer, and the effects of system the parameters are examined. Using Pluronic F-127 as the stabilization agent throughout the study, sub-micron PLA “nanoparticles” with diameters ranging from 200 to 250 nm are produced through solvent displacement, and purified and isolated by repeated centrifugation. abstract: While many natural features are rounded, few techniques exist to create microstructures with rounded features. Here, we describe an approach which uses microcontact printing to pattern molds around water and ice for the creation of 3D rounded microscale features. Microcontact printing is a technique that uses polymer stamps to create patterns of self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) in order to selectively modify the chemical properties of a surface. This process was used to deposit patterns of hexadecanethiol (HDT) on a gold-coated silicon wafer using a microstructured stamp. Mercaptoundecanoic acid (MUA) was used to backfill the remaining surface area, creating a surface with distinctly hydrophobic (HDT) and hydrophilic (MUA) regions. When these surfaces were exposed to water, the liquid localized on the hydrophilic regions of the pattern and could be frozen in place, forming arrays of curved, 3D structures. These patterned ice molds were then cast in polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), forming polymer replicas of the three dimensional surfaces.

title: The Effect of Surface Coating on Magnetic Properties and Local Structure in Coated Cobalt Nanoparticles

authors_text: Natalie Schieber, Eric Formo, Adam J. Rondinone, Thomas Proffen and Mikhail Feygenson
abstract: Magnetic cobalt nanoparticles have potential applications in magnetic data storage devices. They can be arranged densely enough on a substrate to eclipse current data storage methods. At temperatures below the blocking temperature (Tb), these nanoparticles can retain the direction of their magnetic moment even when an applied magnetic field is removed. The direction of each nanoparticle’s magnetic moment corresponds to one bit of information. One challenge to developing these materials is that the Tb for small cobalt nanoparticles is below 10K. One way to increase the Tb is by increasing the surface anisotropy of the nanoparticle with a surface coating. To study this effect, one sample of cobalt nanoparticles was oxidized, forming a CoO shell while another was coated with silicon dioxide to prevent oxidation and serve as a reference to the oxidized sample. The resulting blocking temperatures and local structures were studied. Transmission electron microscopy confirmed the presence of spherical nanoparticles and was used to determine the size distribution. Synchrotron x-ray pair distribution function (PDF) analysis was used to study the effects of coating on the local structure of nanoparticles. The blocking temperature and oxidation state were determined from MPMS magnetometer data. The PDF of the silica coated nanoparticles shows a hexagonal structure, with different lattice constants than the bulk phase. The PDF of the Co/CoO core shell nanoparticles indicates a distorted cubic structure and a large amount of CoO. The magnetization data reveal a Tb of 5K for the silica coated nanoparticles and no trace of oxidation, in contrast to the CoO nanoparticles, where the Tb was 250K.

topic: Glucose-Initiated Accelerated Degradation of Poly (Beta-amino Ester) Hydrogels for Drug Delivery
title: Glucose-Initiated Accelerated Degradation of Poly (Beta-amino Ester) Hydrogels for Drug Delivery

authors_text: Melissa Bianchin Prado, Nathanael A. Stocke and J. Zach Hilt
abstract: Hydrogels have long been used in the development of a range of applications such as intelligent drug delivery systems, tissue engineering, orthopedic implants, and other medical applications. Their three-dimensional structure, formed by crosslinking chains, allows them to absorb large quantities of water, thereby mimicking many soft tissues. Currently, there is a significant interest in intelligent drug delivery systems for the treatment of diabetes, and hydrogels could offer a unique platform for such applications provided they could sense and respond to glucose. For drug delivery, a hydrogel can be loaded with, and subsequently release, a drug in response to environmental stimuli. For degradable hydrogels, this response is the hydrolytic or enzymatic cleavage of chemical bonds resulting in erosion of the three-dimensional network. For biomedical applications, poly (ethylene glycol) (PEG) is one of the most widely used polymers in hydrogels. Additionally, common PEG precursors can be combined with amines to form poly (b-amino ester) (PBAEs) hydrogels that are hydrolytically degradable as opposed to traditionally non-degradable PEG-based hydrogels. This project aims to investigate the rate of glucose-initiated degradation of hydrogels by measuring the mass loss ratio of the gels at different points of time. Macromers used for PBAE hydrogels were synthesized with a diacrylate:primary amine ratio of 1.2:1 using isobutylamine and varying ratios of PEG 400 diacrylate (PEG400DA) and diethylene glycol diacrylate (DEGDA). PBAE hydrogels with were synthesized by UV polymerization with 2,2 – dimethoxy-2-phenylacetophenone as a photoinitiator and DMSO as the solvent. The molar ratios of DEGDA:PEG400DA were varied at 1:1, 3:1 and 10:1 with the latter being the most hydrophobic and therefore displaying the longest degradation profile. Studies show that glucose and glucose oxidase reaction products are able to accelerate the degradation of PBAE hydrogels. The ability to accelerate the degradation of hydrogels by sensing glucose provides a platform for intelligent drug delivery systems composed of biocompatible materials with great potential for biomedical applications.

topic: Thermoelectric Power Generation in Dynamic Temperature Environments
title: Thermoelectric Power Generation in Dynamic Temperature Environments
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Peter Attia, Matthew R. Lewis, Cory C. Bomberger, Ajay K. Prasad and Joshua M. O. Zide
abstract: Thermoelectric materials have long held promise as a critical piece of the sustainable-energy puzzle. The benefits of thermoelectric power are numerous: they capture energy from waste heat (such as that of industrial processes and automobile exhaust) and naturally-occurring thermal gradients (such as geothermal energy), have a small size, degrade slowly, generally consist of nontoxic materials, and operate silently; however, their widespread adaptation has been limited by their low power outputs and efficiencies. Although a large number of thermoelectric applications have been considered, investigated, and commercialized, the thermal driving force remains the same in each: a steady-state, spatial temperature gradient. Here, an alternate source of thermal energy for thermoelectric power – transient thermal gradients, or the fluctuations of an environmental temperature with time – is investigated; this source of power is useful for low-power devices in remote locations. We design and characterize devices that employ a thermoelectric module sandwiched between two heat exchangers with significantly different thermal masses and examine the effects of heat exchanger size and material selection, period of oscillation of the environmental temperature fluctuations, and radiative heat transfer on the thermoelectric power output. We report maximum experimental power generation on the order of milliwatts using standard bismuth telluride thermoelectric modules in devices with a size of about 10 cm 3 .

topic: Discovery of ZnO-Binding Peptides for Photocatalytic Material Synthesis

abstract: Clean air and water are important for sustainable habitats. Improved methods for maintaining and renewing these resources are critical. Photocatalysis is a promising technology for removal of toxic molecules and pollutants from air and water. Photocatalysis utilizes sunlight to activate photosensitive materials to catalyze chemical reactions necessary to degrade pollutants into innocuous compounds. Nanoscale zinc oxide (ZnO) displays optical and electrical properties suitable for photocatalysis. Furthermore, unlike other conventional methods, nanoscale biomineralized ZnO is advantageously manufactured under ambient conditions. The objective of this study was to find a specific peptide that binds to ZnO, with the possibility to biomineralize nanostructures of ZnO in the future. Biopanning, a combinatorial phage display technique with phages displaying approximately 10 7 different peptides, was used to select peptide sequences with affinity for ZnO. After five rounds of biopanning, two phages which showed strong affinity for ZnO were isolated. The peptides VPGAAEHT and DRQVDATA were displayed on these phages. To confirm the affinity of these phages for ZnO, binding tests were completed using a ZnO thin film grown on a silicon substrate as the target material. The identified phages, displaying VPGAAEHT and DRQVDATA peptides, were 79 and 61 times more likely to bind to the ZnO thin film on a silicon substrate target than the wild-type control phage, respectively. Binding studies were also performed using the silicon substrate as a target to ensure the phage affinity was for the ZnO thin film rather than the silicon substrate. The VPGAAEHT phage demonstrated an affinity for the ZnO thin film which was more than twice that observed for the silicon substrate alone, whereas the DRQVDATA phage showed a comparable affinity for both the ZnO thin film and the silicon substrate. These results will benefit future research to biomineralized nanostructured ZnO material which could be used for photocatalytic devices.

abstract: Title: The Effect of Bucky-Ball Nanoparticle Additives on the Electrowetting-on-Dielectric Response of Two Ionic Liquids Abstract for Poster Presentation at the 2013 AIChE Annual Student Conference, November 1-5, San Francisco, California Authors: Glenn R. Hafenstine†, Marriner H. Merrill*‡, and James P. Thomas‡ †Chemical Engineering Department; Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS 66506, USA ‡Multifunctional Materials Branch, Code 6350; Naval Research Laboratory (NRL), Washington, DC 20375, USA *Corresponding Author: marriner.merrill@nrl.navy.mil Abstract: Electrowetting-on-Dielectric (EWOD) is an effective method for manipulating small volumes of liquids in applications such as lab-on-a-chip systems, e-microreactors, and novel multifunctional materials. EWOD uses an applied electrical potential between a drop of conductive liquid and a dielectric-coated electrode (on a solid substrate) to effect changes in the liquid-solid contact angle. As the potential is applied, it tends to “spread” the drop out over the drop-substrate interface regions that are electroded, decreasing the contact angle. Ionic liquids are often used in EWOD applications due to their low vapor pressures (non-evaporating) and their wide range of available chemistries. In this work, we evaluate the effect of adding nanoparticles (diameters ranging from 1 to 100’s nm) on the EWOD response (contact angle change with applied potential) for several ionic liquids over a 0 to +/- 200 V applied potential range. Previous research on a dispersion of 7.7 nm quantum dots in an aqueous solvent reported significantly enhanced EWOD response over that predicted by the Lippmann-Young equation. Of the various nanoparticle-IL’s tested in our work, the 0.05 wt% solution of 0.71-nm ‘bucky-balls’ in 1-Butyl-2,3-dimethylimidazolium nitrate (MMBI-NO 3 ) showed the best improvement in EWOD response (23% decrease in actuating voltage for the same contact angle change). The same nanoparticles added to 1-Ethyl-3-methylimidazolium methyl sulfate (MEI-MeSO 4 ), however, showed only slight improvement in EWOD response. At this stage of the research, we do not fully understand the role played by the bucky-ball additives in improving EWOD response with the MMBI-NO 3 nor the reason no improvement in response was observed with the bucky-ball additives in MEI-MeSO 4 . Ion chemistry, and nanoparticle dispersion quality and segregation within the droplet are potential mechanisms being investigated. Further testing with several different ionic liquids of varied cations and anions is being conducted to answer these questions.

abstract: Samantha Jones, Andrzej Latka, and Sidney R. Nagel When a drop of liquid impacts a solid surface it will splash emitting tiny droplets. This phenomenon results from a variety of complex interactions between the liquid and the substrate. Surprisingly, when air pressure is reduced splashing is completely suppressed [1-3]. The mechanism by which air induces splashing is still unexplained and the question remains: where does the air matter? In this project we consider the air at the advancing edge of the spreading drop. This was done by studying the dynamic contact angle between the spreading liquid and the solid surface. Using high-speed videos of drop impacts, we measured the evolution of the dynamic contact angle for water/glycerol drops of different viscosities. abstract: Innovative nanoelectromechanical (NEM) switches are being developed to reduce device actuation voltages as well as to avoid adhesion, which results in device failures. Minimizing leakage currents and increasing device longevity are additional goals of this technology. Unlike traditional electromechanical switches, which rely on direct contact of the electrodes, these switches contain a nanometer-scale organic thin film between two electrodes. The current is modulated by compressing the film, which decreases the gap to a dimension where tunneling between the two electrodes occurs. Conversely, the switch is turned off by the restoring force of the organic layer that returns the gap to its original distance. We term this squeezable switch a “squitch”. The properties of the squitch are highly dependent on the organic material sandwiched between the electrodes. Modified poly(3-hexylthiophene-2,5-diyl) (P3HT) was explored for the design of this organic layer due to its conductive properties and previous use in devices. A simple, two-step, post-polymerization procedure developed in the Swager group was used for the modification of P3HT. This procedure involves bromination of P3HT with N -bromosuccinimide followed by lithium-halogen exchange and quenching of the anion with an electrophile. Through this work we found that anhydrides were the electrophile of choice to yield ketone-modified P3HT. Several functional groups, including long, branched, and unsaturated alkyl chains, trimethylsilyl, and triisopropylsilyl groups were installed on P3HT by varying the anhydride structure. Additionally, a para-substituent study of synthesized benzoyl-modified P3HT was conducted to gain insight into how the ketone modification alters the properties of the polymer.

abstract: This research focused on the development and use of a novel methodology to study corrosion under aqueous electrolyte drops ranging in diameter from 20-1000μm, the most common aerosol size range found in coastal marine locations. The objective of this work was to examine the relationship between drop size and corrosion attack of bare low carbon steel under simulated atmospheric marine conditions. It has been recently reported in the literature that corrosion rate appears to be a function of deposited aerosol drop size; however, empirical data are insufficient to establish a strong, quantitative correlation between drop size and corrosion rate. For this work, a drop-on-demand inkjet printer was custom built by coupling a commercial jetting device with a programmable two-axis stage. Singular droplets of aqueous sodium chloride were deposited on polished 1010 steel substrates followed by exposure to 75% relative humidity for 24 hours. It was found that, in general, the volume loss increased with drop diameter according to a power law. Various attack morphologies were observed; attack was primarily filiform for drops 20-100μm in diameter whereas deep, separate pits formed under drops 300-1000μm in diameter. Filiform attack is characterized by shallow pits that occur under and travel outside of the initial drop area. Corrosion always occurred for drops greater than 150μm in diameter, but was not consistently observed under drops in the 20-100μm range. The fraction of drops that showed no corrosion increased with decreasing drop size below 100μm in diameter. However, drops smaller than 100μm that corroded were found to have the greatest volume loss compared to their salt loading density. The results from this study suggest that the manner and geometry in which salt is deposited onto a surface will significantly affect corrosion loss along with the mode of attack. From a technical standpoint, these results suggest that service life prediction approaches including accelerated testing have the potential to more accurately simulate natural atmospheres if electrolyte geometry is taken into account.

abstract: Shape Memory Polymer Nanofoams L. Smith 1 , A.P. Soliani 2 , I. Luzinov 2 1 Biomedical, Chemical, and Materials Engineering, San Jose State University, 95192 2 Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Clemson University, 29634 The purpose of the current research is to investigate the effects of cross-linking on the formation and response of a shape memory nanofoam polymer material. The evaluation has been conducted through a foaming process and the response of said material to various analytes. In essence, the project investigates different polymers with various chemical functionalities and different number of available epoxy groups to create a specific and selective shape memory material that will be able to sense (“respond”) in a unique way to various analytes. The shape memory behavior of the system will be imparted by nature of the anchoring layers containing different amounts of reactive epoxy groups. The investigated anchoring layers were poly (glycidyl methacrylate) (PGMA) and a random copolymer composed of 70:30 poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) and PGMA, respectively. The anchoring layer was further functionalized with low molecular weight carboxy- terminated polystyrene (PS) by grafting. The polymer was deposited via dip-coating technique and annealed at five temperatures to achieve different PS thicknesses grafted to the anchoring layer. To monitor the changes in thickness and morphology of the system, reflectometry and atomic force microscope (AFM) were used. Initial results indicate that the layers were successfully synthesized, foamed, and showed a specific and different response when exposed to a number of analytes in a sequential manner. topic: Anti-Biofouling Performance of Slippery, Lubricant-Infused Swollen Silicone Tubing
title: Anti-Biofouling Performance of Slippery, Lubricant-Infused Swollen Silicone Tubing
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Materials Engineering and Sciences
authors_text: Noah W. Cowan MacCallum, Ronn Friedlander, Derek Sun, Tak-Sing Wong, Benjamin D. Hatton, Philseok Kim and Joanna Aizenberg
abstract: With the rise of multi- and pan-drug resistant organisms resulting from overuse of antibiotic-based treatments, preventing nosocomial infections is a timely and important goal. While biofilm formation on urinary catheters remains a leading cause of nosocomial infection, an effective fix remains elusive. Swelling of poly-dimethy siloxane (silicone) in silicone oil produces a slippery, hydrophobic, and extremely flat liquid surface layer that surrounds the solid polymer surface. We evaluated the anti-biofouling performance of this inexpensive and simple modification of an existing catheter material. Using Pseudomonas aeruginosa as a model organism, we quantified biofilm growth on swollen and un-swollen silicone by quantitative crystal violet assay and found an 8-fold reduction in biofilm formation on swollen silicone at lower shear rates (10 s -1 , 47.8 s -1 ) and a 134-fold reduction at the highest tested shear rate (270.4 s -1 ) after 48h of closed-loop culture. Further, a simple, 5s washing step almost entirely removes any traces of a biofilm present on the swollen tubing. Confocal imaging confirms that biofilm formation is substantially reduced on swollen silicone. Given the excellent anti-biofouling performance, simplicity of manufacture, inexpensive production, and even improvements to patient comfort, this approach shows significant potential to be clinically implemented and subsequently reduce worldwide incidence of catheter-associated infections.
